about: Two hundred short original books for Eden's shelves (SA-E12, #2927): an id, a title, tags and the first page. A book (eden:book) carries its title and first page by reference to a row here; which shelf holds which books is content/worlds/eden/stock.json. Rows are only appended: a published id keeps its text.

books.title: The Lamplighter's Last Summer
books.first_page: Every evening for forty-one years, Osric Vale had walked the canal path with his long brass pole and a pocket full of matches. Tonight the council letter sat folded in his coat, warm against his ribs like a small animal. Electric lamps, it said. Progress, it said. Very grateful for your service. He lit the first lamp by the footbridge and watched the flame settle into its glass. A girl on the bridge was watching him too, chin on her arms, feet dangling over the dark water. 'Do they ever go out by themselves?' she asked. Osric considered lying. Instead he told her the truth: that one lamp, the one by the old mill, had never needed him at all.

books.title: Letters from the Harbour Wall
books.first_page: Dear Tamsin, you will laugh, but I am writing this sitting on the harbour wall with my feet in a bucket. The bucket is not mine. It belongs to a fisherman named Ebb who says I may borrow it until the tide turns, and that I look like someone who needs a bucket. I arrived in Gullhaven on Tuesday with two suitcases and no plan, exactly as you predicted. The rooms above the chandlery smell of rope and lemon soap. The landlady has a parrot that only says 'Not today.' I have not cried once, which you will also not believe. Tomorrow I am going to ask about the job at the net loft. Wish me courage. Yours from the edge of everything, Bea.

books.title: A Map of Small Kindnesses
books.first_page: I started the map on the day my mother left me her house and nothing else. Not money, not an explanation, just the narrow house on Wicker Row and a drawer full of pencils. The first mark was a small green circle where the baker had pressed a warm roll into my hand and refused payment. The second was a blue triangle by the canal, where a stranger had fished my hat out of the water with an umbrella. By the end of the first month the paper was crowded with symbols, and I had begun to notice something odd. The marks were not scattered at all. They were making a path, and the path led straight back to my own front door.

books.title: The Ferryman's Daughter Sings
books.first_page: Nobody on the lake had heard Mira Fallow sing since she was nine, and she was twenty-six now, which made it a long silence even for a family famous for keeping quiet. Her father rowed the ferry between Reedmouth and the island. She kept the tickets, mended the oars and counted the coins into a tin shaped like a fish. Then, one grey morning, a passenger with a cello case and a sunburned nose sat in the stern and began, very softly, to hum a tune Mira knew. It was her mother's tune. Nobody outside the family was supposed to know it. Mira dropped the tin, and forty coins rolled into the bilge.

books.title: Seven Teacups and a Storm
books.first_page: Aunt Prudence owned seven teacups and invited nine people, a mathematics she described as 'optimistic.' Trouble in Hobb's End usually started that way. The guests arrived just as the sky turned the colour of a bruised plum. Mr Danning brought his own cup, which was considered rude. The postmaster's cousin brought a dog, which was considered worse. By the time the first thunder rolled over the hills, the parlour held nine guests, one dog, seven cups and a single plate of scones that Aunt Prudence guarded like a general. Then the lamps flickered and went out. When they came back on, a full minute later, every guest was exactly where they had been, and the scones were gone.

books.title: The Cartographer of Puddles
books.first_page: My job, if you can call it a job, is to draw the puddles of Eastmere after every rain. The town council pays me in soup tickets and a small room above the clock shop. Nobody remembers why the post exists. I suspect it was invented by a mayor with a sense of humour and never abolished by anyone with the courage to ask. I take it seriously anyway. Puddles, I have learned, are not random. They gather where the road remembers being a stream. They linger where children like to jump. And last Thursday, after the long autumn storm, a puddle appeared on Saddler Street that had no business being there, because Saddler Street is the highest road in town.

books.title: What the Canal Remembers
books.first_page: Five generations of the Corvell family had lived beside the north canal, and each generation had dropped something into it. Great-great-grandfather Silas dropped a wedding ring, on purpose, after an argument he later regretted. His daughter dropped a key. Her son dropped a whole bicycle, which was still talked about at weddings. When the canal was drained for repairs in the spring that Nell Corvell turned sixty, the whole family gathered on the bank in their good coats, pretending they had only come for the fresh air. Nell stood a little apart, holding her grandson's hand. She was the only one who knew what she herself had dropped, forty years ago, and she was hoping very hard that it had sunk too deep to find.

books.title: The Beekeeper's Second Chance
books.first_page: Hester Orme had not planned to fall in love at fifty-three, and certainly not with a man who was afraid of bees. Yet there he was at her garden gate, the new schoolteacher, holding a jar of her honey as if it might go off like a firework. 'I wanted to say,' he began, then stopped, because a bee had landed on his sleeve. Hester waited. The bee walked the length of his cuff with great seriousness. He did not move. He did not swat. He simply went very pale and very polite. 'It likes you,' she said. 'I doubt that,' he whispered. 'It is only looking for the way out.' Hester laughed for the first time that summer.

books.title: Grandmother Fennick's Recipe Box
books.first_page: When Grandmother Fennick died, she left the farmhouse to my uncle, the orchard to my mother and the recipe box to me, which caused a great deal more argument than the orchard. It was an ordinary tin box, dented on one corner, painted with faded cherries. Inside were two hundred cards in her small slanting hand. Plum dumplings. Nettle soup. Something called Thursday Pie, which nobody in the family had ever eaten. I was fifteen and could barely boil an egg. My cousins said it was wasted on me. That night I read every card by torchlight, and on the back of the very last one, under a recipe for lemon curd, she had written my name and four words: start with the pie.

books.title: The Ghost in the Reading Room
books.first_page: Quill Square library closes at six, but the ghost does not seem to know this. I am the night caretaker, so I would know. Every evening at a quarter past seven, the reading lamp at table four switches itself on, and a book appears there, open, though I have shelved every book myself and locked every door. At first I was frightened. Then I was curious. Now, to be honest, I am a little offended, because the ghost has terrible taste. Last week it was a manual on drainage. On Monday it was a seed catalogue from thirty years ago. Tonight, though, the book on table four was mine. My own childhood diary, which I burned in the garden when I was twelve.

books.title: Courtyard of the Blue Door
books.first_page: Six households shared the courtyard behind the blue door, and they shared it the way cats share a sunny step: politely, with occasional hissing. There was a fig tree in the middle that belonged to everyone and was argued over by all. There was a well that no longer gave water but still received wishes. There was old Mr Abernath on the ground floor, who fed the sparrows, and the Pellow twins upstairs, who chased them. There were washing lines, bicycles, a bench with one short leg and a great many opinions. And then, one wet morning in October, there was a stranger in the courtyard with a wheelbarrow, a letter of ownership and a plan to cut down the fig.

books.title: A Kite Over Thistle Hill
books.first_page: I was eleven the summer my brother Rafe built the kite, and he was fourteen and certain of everything. It was taller than both of us, made from bedsheets and broom handles and a great deal of string borrowed without asking. Mother said it would never fly. Father said it would fly straight into the duck pond. Rafe said nothing, which was how I knew he was nervous. We carried it up Thistle Hill at dawn while the grass was still wet. The wind came off the lake in long cool breaths. I held the string, Rafe held the kite, and when he shouted 'Now!' I ran, and the ground let go of me.

books.title: The Clockmaker's Apprentice Runs Away
books.first_page: Pip Larrow left the clockmaker's shop at four in the morning with a loaf of bread, a screwdriver and the one thing she was absolutely forbidden to touch. It was a pocket watch with no hands. Master Gribble kept it in a velvet box on the highest shelf and wound it every Sunday, though it told no time at all. Pip had asked about it exactly once and been sent to sweep the cellar for a week. Now the watch ticked in her pocket like a second heart. She slipped through the market before the stalls were up and reached the harbour as the first boats were leaving. Only then did she notice that the watch had grown hands. Both of them were pointing out to sea.

books.title: Dear Neighbour, About the Goat
books.first_page: Dear Neighbour at Number Fourteen, I hope this note finds you well. I am writing about the goat. I do not wish to be unkind, and I understand that a goat is a living creature with its own opinions. However, it has now eaten three of my tea towels, one doormat and the left sleeve of my husband's good jacket while he was still wearing it. It also stands on my garden wall every morning at six and shouts. I have tried shouting back. This did not help. Could we perhaps meet to discuss a fence? I will bring biscuits. Please do not bring the goat. Yours sincerely, Agatha Brindle, Number Twelve. PS. It is on my roof again.

books.title: The Last Boat to Wrenmouth
books.first_page: 'No more boats to Wrenmouth until spring,' said the harbourmaster, with the satisfaction of a man who had been waiting all year to say it. Lorne Ashby set down her bag and looked out at the grey water. Somewhere across it was the island where her grandfather lived alone, and somewhere on that island was a letter he had written but never sent. The telegram had said only: come before the ice. 'Is there anyone,' she asked, 'who might take me anyway?' The harbourmaster laughed. Then he stopped laughing, and his eyes slid toward the end of the pier, where a small red boat was moored and an old woman sat mending a sail.

books.title: Saltwater and Marmalade
books.first_page: Juniper Vance ran the smallest cafe in Port Linnet, which had four tables and a door that stuck in wet weather. She made the best marmalade on the coast and the worst coffee, and she knew both of these things. Every morning at seven a fisherman named Cal came in, ordered the coffee, drank it without complaint and left a coin and a shell on the counter. She had a jar of shells now, nearly full. She had never asked him why. Then, on the first day of the herring season, Cal did not come in. At half past seven, Juniper found herself standing at the window. At eight, she was walking down to the harbour with a jar of marmalade, telling herself it was only neighbourly.

books.title: The Year of the Tall Hedge
books.first_page: In the year the hedge grew taller than the bell tower, the village of Dimbley divided itself neatly into two camps. One camp believed the hedge should be cut. The other camp belonged to Mrs Orla Tunstall, who had planted it, and who sat beneath it each afternoon in a deckchair with a pair of shears across her knees, daring anyone to try. Nobody knew why the hedge grew so fast. Some blamed the rain. Some blamed the compost. Young Teddy Marsh, who delivered the post, privately blamed the strange humming that came from the hedge after dark, but Teddy was nine and nobody asked his opinion. That turned out to be a mistake.

books.title: A Pocketful of River Stones
books.first_page: Ada collects one stone from the river each day she is sad, and by March her coat pockets are so heavy she walks with a slight lean. Her neighbour notices first. He is a retired surveyor called Tomas who notices angles for a living, or used to. 'You are listing to port,' he says over the fence. Ada tells him about the stones. She expects him to say something sensible about grief, or worse, about coats. Instead he goes inside and comes back with a wooden bowl. 'For the ones you are ready to put down,' he says. She does not use it that day, or the next. But on the third morning she sets a single grey stone in the bowl, and the bowl, quite clearly, sets it back.

books.title: The Quiet Tenant of Number Nine
books.first_page: Nobody on Lantern Street had seen the tenant of number nine, though everybody had theories. The milk was taken in each morning. The window boxes were watered. The rent, according to the landlord, was paid in coins wrapped neatly in brown paper and left on the step. Mrs Halloway at number seven thought it was a retired actress hiding from her public. The Dunmore boys thought it was a bear. I thought nothing about it at all, until the evening I came home to find a brown paper parcel on my own step, addressed to me in careful pencil. Inside was the harmonica I had lost in the canal when I was seven. It had been cleaned and polished, and someone had tuned it.

books.title: Mapping the Wind
books.first_page: Three people, one balloon and a dog who had not been consulted: that was the whole expedition. Professor Imelda Strand was the leader, because the balloon was hers. Her nephew Basil was the navigator, because he owned a compass. And Pudding, a brown spaniel of uncertain age, was ballast. Their goal was simple. They would rise above the hills of Calder and follow the autumn wind wherever it went, drawing it as they flew, until they had made the first true map of the air. The townsfolk gathered in the park to watch them leave. Several brought sandwiches. Nobody, including the professor, had thought to ask how the balloon would come down.

books.title: The Orchard Keeper's Diary
books.first_page: First of April. The pear trees are budding, and so, I think, am I. Fifty-eight years old and I have just signed the papers for an orchard I cannot afford, on a hill I have only seen twice, in a valley where nobody knows my name. My sister says I have lost my senses. Perhaps. But I stood under those old trees in the rain last month and felt something I have not felt since I was a girl. Second of April. Discovered the roof leaks. Discovered the well is full of frogs. Discovered a man asleep in the barn who says he came with the orchard. He has a letter to prove it, signed by the previous owner and dated forty years ago.

books.title: Two Chairs on the Jetty
books.first_page: Two chairs stand at the end of the jetty in Sallow Bay, and for thirty years they belonged to Morwen and Albert Keel. Every evening, rain or shine, the couple walked down with a flask and a blanket and sat watching the boats come home. When Albert died in the winter, the village expected Morwen to stop going. She did not. She went alone, sat in her chair, and poured two cups from the flask. People were kind about it. They left her be. Then, in April, a young man arrived in the village with a rucksack and a sunburn, and one evening, knowing none of this, he walked to the end of the jetty and sat down in Albert's chair.

books.title: The Lantern Festival Mix-Up
books.first_page: There are three rules for the Lantern Festival in Millbrook, and in a single evening the Pemberley family managed to break all of them. Rule one: lanterns must be made of paper. Rule two: each lantern must carry a wish written by its owner. Rule three: no one, under any circumstances, may read another person's wish. It was the third rule that caused the most trouble, because when the wind changed and blew the whole flotilla of lanterns back onto the village green, every wish in Millbrook landed face up in the wet grass. And the one that landed at the mayor's feet was written in the unmistakable handwriting of his own mother.

books.title: Snow Comes to Larkspur Lane
books.first_page: You will remember the winter the snow came to Larkspur Lane, because it had never come before and it has never come since. You were seven. You woke to a silence so thick you thought you had gone deaf, and you ran to the window in your socks. The canal was white. The rooftops were white. Mr Fosse's wheelbarrow, left out overnight as always, was now a small white hill. Your mother stood in the kitchen doorway holding a pan she had forgotten she was holding. 'Well,' she said, and nothing else. Then someone knocked at the door, and you opened it, and there on the step stood a snowman who had very clearly done the knocking.

books.title: The Bell That Rang Backwards
books.first_page: Sixty years had passed since the bell in the old harbour tower last rang, which is why everyone in Corran heard it the night it did. It rang at midnight. It rang thirteen times. And on the thirteenth stroke, those who were awake swore the sound did not fade away into the dark but came rushing back toward them, as though the bell were drawing a deep breath. Ivo Penhallow, who kept the tower key on a nail by his stove, went up in his slippers with a lantern. He found the rope coiled neatly on the floor, the dust on every stair undisturbed, and a single small wet footprint on the top step, pointing down.

books.title: A Garden for Absent Friends
books.first_page: After the move, Wren planted one thing for every person she had left behind. A rosemary bush for her grandmother, because it was stubborn and smelled of kitchens. Sweet peas for her old friend Lila, who never stopped talking. A row of sunflowers for the boys from the football team, who were loud and tall and turned their faces toward whatever was most exciting. Her new garden behind the canal house was small, and soon it was crowded. Her mother said it was a lovely way to remember. Wren said nothing. She was watching the bare patch in the corner where something had come up on its own, something she had not planted, with leaves she did not recognise.

books.title: The Tinker and the Tidewife
books.first_page: In the days when the coast road was still a mud track, a tinker named Joss came walking into the fishing village of Skerry with a cart full of pans and a head full of debts. He meant to stay one night. He stayed seven years, and this is the story of why. It began with a kettle. The kettle belonged to the Tidewife, who lived alone in a cottage below the cliffs that the sea reached twice a day and somehow never flooded. She came to his cart at dusk, set the kettle down, and said, 'This has a hole in it. Mend it, and I will pay you in anything but money.' Joss, being a fool, said yes.

books.title: Stepping Stones Across the Lake
books.first_page: There are twenty-two stepping stones across the narrow end of Cleave Lake, and in summer they sit just above the water. Every child in the village crosses them sooner or later. It is the thing you do to prove you are no longer small. I was thirteen and I had not done it, and Dara Quell had done it at nine and never let me forget it. So on the last afternoon of the holidays I went down to the lake alone, took off my shoes and stepped onto the first stone. It was warm from the sun. The second was cold. By the eleventh I realised there were not twenty-two stones that day. There were twenty-three, and the extra one was moving.

books.title: The Brothers Hollin and the Wager
books.first_page: Amos and Barnaby Hollin had not spoken to each other in nine years, which was difficult, because they ran the same boatyard and shared a single kettle. They communicated by notes pinned to the workbench. The notes had become, over time, a kind of literature. 'Your saw is in my light.' 'Your light is in my way.' 'The kettle is not a democracy.' The whole harbour knew about the silence, and most people quietly enjoyed it. Then one spring morning a stranger arrived with a purse of silver and an order for the fastest rowing boat on the coast. He wanted it in thirty days. He wanted it built by both brothers. And he wanted to know which of them was the better craftsman.

books.title: Cake for the Whole Valley
books.first_page: Bettina Moss had promised to bake a cake for the whole valley, and the whole valley, it turned out, was rather larger than she had pictured when she said it. She had pictured perhaps forty people. The parish list said three hundred and twelve, not counting the shepherds on the high pastures, who would certainly come down if they smelled sugar. The harvest fair was in nine days. Her oven held two tins. Her flour bin held enough for one modest sponge. Bettina sat at her kitchen table with a pencil and a cup of tea gone cold, and slowly began to draw what she needed: not a recipe, but a map of every kitchen in the valley.

books.title: The Night Market Violinist
books.first_page: At the night market by the east canal, between the stall that sells paper birds and the stall that sells hot chestnuts, a woman plays the violin. She has played there every Friday for three years. She never speaks. She never takes requests. She keeps her case shut and accepts no coins, and when people try to give them, she shakes her head and nods toward the chestnut seller, who sells more chestnuts on Fridays than on any other night. I am the chestnut seller. I have never learned her name. And tonight, for the first time in three years, she stopped in the middle of a tune, lowered her bow, and looked straight at me.

books.title: Fog over Pellow Marsh
books.first_page: Fog came in over Pellow Marsh at four in the afternoon, which was early even for November, and with it came the sound of someone whistling. Gideon Rook heard it from his kitchen. He put down his knife and went to the door. The marsh was a white wall. The path to the village had vanished. The whistling went on, a cheerful little tune, very slightly out of key, moving slowly from left to right as if someone were walking along the dyke. Gideon knew the tune. He had whistled it himself, every evening as a boy, walking home along that same dyke. He had not whistled it in fifty years. He had, in fact, forgotten it until now.

books.title: The Hat That Would Not Stay
books.first_page: Mr Percival Dunwiddy bought the hat on a Tuesday, lost it on a Wednesday and spent the rest of the summer chasing it across the county. It was a fine hat. Green felt, a jaunty feather, a brim exactly as wide as a dinner plate. The milliner had looked at it with an odd expression and said, 'Are you quite sure, sir?' Mr Dunwiddy had been quite sure. He was less sure the next morning, when a light breeze lifted the hat from his head on the canal bridge, carried it over three rooftops and set it down gently on the head of a scarecrow in the allotments. The scarecrow, he would later learn, was the hat's previous owner.

books.title: A Summer of Borrowed Bicycles
books.first_page: Not one person in Finchcombe Cross owned a bicycle that summer. They borrowed them. It started when old Mrs Garrow put her late husband's bicycle by her gate with a sign that said: take it, bring it back. Then the postman did the same. Then the school. By June there were forty bicycles moving around the village and nobody could say for certain whose was whose. I was sixteen and had just failed every exam I had taken. My parents were not speaking to me, and I was not speaking to anyone. Every morning I took whatever bicycle was nearest and rode until the roads ran out. On the twelfth of July, the bicycle I took had a note tucked in the basket.

books.title: The Weaver's Unfinished Blanket
books.first_page: On the loom in the attic of the Tarrow house there is a blanket that has been woven by four generations of women and finished by none of them. It is very long now. It hangs from the loom and folds across the floorboards and climbs, in neat coils, halfway up the far wall. Each woman worked her own colours into it. Great-grandmother Elsbeth wove in grey and green. Grandmother Ros wove in red. My mother wove in a blue so bright it looks wet. I am nineteen. The loom passed to me last winter, and with it a single instruction written on a card pinned to the frame: do not finish it until you know why we stopped.

books.title: Postcards to the Lighthouse
books.first_page: To the Keeper, Hollow Point Light. Dear Keeper, you do not know me. I live in the village across the bay, in the yellow house with the crooked chimney, and every night I watch your light go round. I have done this since I was small. Tonight my father told me the lighthouse is to be made automatic, and that you will be leaving. I do not know if that is true. I wanted to say thank you, in case it is. I counted once, and your light has gone round about four million times in my lifetime. That seems like a great deal of work for one person. Please write back if you have time. From Ottilie, age ten. PS. Is it lonely?

books.title: The Mountain Hut Guestbook
books.first_page: Entry, the first of June: Arrived soaked. Stove works, eventually. Somebody has left half a jar of honey and a note that says do not eat the honey. Did not eat the honey. Marta and Jon. Entry, the fourth of June: Thank you to Marta and Jon for not eating the honey. It is for the bear. Kind regards, the Warden. Entry, the fourth of June, later: There is no warden. Signed, the actual warden. Entry, the ninth of June: Can confirm there is a bear. Did not eat the honey. Neither did the bear. Bear seemed disappointed in all of us. Entry, the tenth of June: Who keeps writing these? I have been alone up here for a week.

books.title: Four Sisters and a Houseboat
books.first_page: Our parents named the houseboat the Patience, which our father said was a joke and our mother said was a warning. When they both went away for a year to study lichens, they left it to the four of us, moored on the long canal below the market, with a list of instructions pinned to the galley wall. Rule one: do not untie the boat. Rule two: do not untie the boat. Rule three: we mean it. Clementine, the eldest, read the list aloud with great seriousness. Wick, the youngest, asked what would happen if we did. Nobody answered her. By Thursday we had untied the boat, and by Friday we were three villages downstream and had acquired a heron.

books.title: The Shy Dragon of Coldbrook
books.first_page: The dragon who lived above Coldbrook was, by every account, the shyest creature in the hills. She had not breathed fire in a hundred years. She did not raid farms or hoard gold. She collected thimbles, which villagers left on a flat rock at the foot of her valley, and in return she kept the frost off the orchards with her warm, enormous breath. This arrangement had lasted three generations and suited everyone. Then the new schoolmistress arrived, a brisk young woman named Ivy Harker, who did not believe in dragons, and who on her very first Saturday climbed up the valley with a notebook to prove it. She came down at dusk, white to the lips, and asked where she might buy more thimbles.

books.title: Morning Bread on Cobble Street
books.first_page: At five every morning the bakery on Cobble Street opens, and at five past five Mr Abel Danforth arrives for his bread. He has done this for twelve years. He buys one small brown loaf and asks the baker the same question: 'Anything new today?' And every morning Rosa, the baker, says, 'Only the bread.' It has become a kind of ritual between them, the way a bell becomes part of a door. Rosa has never told him that she bakes the small brown loaf for him alone, that nobody else buys it. This morning, at five past five, the door opened and a girl of about eight walked in, put three coins on the counter and said, very carefully, 'Grandad says, anything new today?'

books.title: The Case of the Missing Marrow
books.first_page: Somebody stole the prize marrow from the Ashcombe show tent between half past nine and ten o'clock on Saturday morning, and by eleven the whole village was a crime scene. The marrow belonged to Colonel Ffinch, who had grown it for eight months, measured it daily and sung to it, according to his housekeeper, in a fine baritone. It weighed nineteen pounds. It could not have been slipped into a pocket. Yet the tent had one entrance, guarded throughout by the chairwoman of the show committee and a very attentive terrier. Dot Pennywhistle, retired schoolteacher, arrived at the tent at five past eleven with a magnifying glass and a flask of tea. 'Right,' she said. 'Who here owns a wheelbarrow?'

books.title: Who Moved the Sundial
books.first_page: For a hundred and twenty years the sundial in Merrow Park had told the time five minutes slow, and the people of Merrow had arranged their lives around it. The baker opened five minutes late. The school bell rang five minutes late. Even the ducks, it was said, arrived for their crusts on sundial time. So when Constable Ada Fenn came to work on Monday and found that the sundial now told the time exactly right, she knew at once that something was very wrong. Someone had moved it. Someone had dug it up in the night, turned it a quarter of an inch, and set it down again without crushing a single tulip. The question was why.

books.title: The Library Card Puzzle
books.first_page: Every book in the Thornbury library has a card in a paper pocket inside the back cover, and every card lists, in faded stamps, the dates it was borrowed. Mostly nobody looks. Librarian Hollis Grey looks. It is, she would say, the most interesting reading in the building. That is how she noticed that eleven different books, on eleven different subjects, had all been borrowed on the same eleven Tuesdays, stretching back nine years, and that not one of those Tuesdays matched a day the library had actually been open. Somebody had been taking books out of a locked building. More curiously, somebody had been bringing them back.

books.title: The Vanishing Prize Rooster
books.first_page: Lord Barrowmere was a rooster, and he had won Best in Show at the Harrowdale Fair four years running, which had made him enemies. On the morning of the fifth fair, his coop was empty. The latch was closed. The straw was undisturbed. A single bronze feather lay on the floor beside a peppermint wrapper and a muddy button. His owner, the formidable Mrs Gillespie, summoned her nephew Arthur from the cafe, where he had been reading a detective novel and eating a bun. 'You read those things,' she said. 'Now solve one.' Arthur had never solved anything more serious than a jigsaw. He picked up the button, turned it over, and recognised it at once.

books.title: The Riddle of the Locked Greenhouse
books.first_page: The greenhouse at the botanical college was locked at six each evening by Professor Lindqvist herself, who carried the only key on a ribbon round her neck. At seven the next morning, she unlocked it to find that every orchid in the building had been turned to face the north wall. Not moved. Not damaged. Turned, each pot rotated precisely, as if the plants had all decided overnight to look away from something. Nothing was missing. No window was broken. The soil in the beds was smooth. Student assistant Tobias Marle, who was fond of puzzles and terrified of the professor, made a list of everyone who could have done it. It was a very short list. It contained only his own name.

books.title: Inspector Quayle and the Stolen Bell
books.first_page: On a Tuesday, during the one hour of the week when the school on Gannet Hill was entirely silent, its bell was stolen. It was the hour of the long division examination. Forty children and two teachers swore they heard nothing. The bell weighed as much as a small pony. It had hung in its frame above the playground for eighty years, and now the frame stood empty, with the rope still dangling. Inspector Quayle, who was sixty-one and had hoped for a quiet week, stood beneath it with his hands behind his back for a long time. Then he asked to see the examination papers. 'All of them?' said the headmistress. 'All of them,' said Quayle. 'I should like to know who finished first.'

books.title: The Thirteenth Jar of Jam
books.first_page: Every autumn Winifred Oakes made exactly twelve jars of damson jam, one for each household on Pudding Lane, and every year she delivered them on the first Sunday of October. This year, when she went down to her larder to collect them, she counted thirteen. She counted again. Thirteen. The extra jar was identical to the others: the same glass, the same gingham lid, the same label in her own handwriting. Except that she had not written it. Winifred sat down on the larder step and considered this with the calm of a woman who had once been the best bookkeeper in the county. Somebody had made a jar of her jam. The question was who, and the question after that was why.

books.title: A Footprint on the Windowsill
books.first_page: I have been the postmistress of Little Hensham for twenty-two years, and I know every boot in the village by its print. That is not a boast. It is simply what happens when you sweep the same doorstep every morning. So when I found a single muddy footprint on the inside of my sorting room windowsill on Thursday, I knew at once that it belonged to nobody who lived here. It was small and narrow, with a star pressed into the heel. The window had been locked. The letters had not been touched. But one parcel, addressed to old Mr Thackery at the mill, had been very carefully unwrapped, and then very carefully wrapped up again, with the string tied in a different knot.

books.title: The Harbourmaster's Cipher
books.first_page: When Harbourmaster Gwilym Rees retired, he left his successor a tide table, a brass telescope and a ledger full of numbers that made no sense at all. The tide table was ordinary. The telescope was dented. But the ledger, which ran to three hundred pages, contained nothing but columns of figures in green ink, one line for every day of his forty years in the job. Young Nia Carrow, the new harbourmaster, assumed at first that they were weights of cargo. Then she noticed that the figures for every midsummer day were exactly the same. And the figures for the night of the great storm, eleven years ago, had been written twice, the second time in red.

books.title: The Curious Case of the Cafe Spoons
books.first_page: The spoons began disappearing from the Copper Kettle cafe on the first of the month, one a day, always a teaspoon, always between the lunchtime rush and closing. By the twentieth, the owner, Mrs Ilse Brandt, was serving tea with forks and her patience was gone. She suspected her customers. Her customers suspected each other. The cafe cat, a large ginger tom named Captain, was suspected by everyone and seemed to enjoy it. It was the Saturday girl, Hattie Lune, who thought to write down every customer, every table and every hour in the back of her maths book. By Friday she had found the pattern. By Saturday she had found the spoons, all twenty, arranged in a perfect circle where nobody had thought to look.

books.title: Pip and the Lantern Boat
books.first_page: Pip was a small grey duckling with one feather that stuck up like a question mark. Every evening the canal folk set paper lanterns afloat, and every evening Pip watched them drift past the reeds, glowing orange and gold. 'Where do they go?' Pip asked her mother. 'Down to the harbour,' said her mother, 'and then nobody knows.' That night Pip could not sleep. The lanterns bobbed and winked as if they were calling her name. So when the moon came up over the courtyard roofs, Pip paddled out from the nest, very quietly, and followed the last lantern under the little stone bridge.

books.title: The Hedgehog Who Collected Buttons
books.first_page: Under the hawthorn hedge at the edge of the park lived a hedgehog called Nettle, and Nettle loved buttons. Red buttons, blue buttons, buttons shaped like flowers, and one very old button with an anchor on it. He found them in the grass after picnics and beside the benches after the market closed. He kept them in a walnut shell, then in a teacup, then in a boot, because the collection kept growing. One morning Nettle counted them all, and there were ninety-nine. 'Just one more,' he whispered, 'and I will have a hundred.' And off he trundled, nose to the ground, to find it.

books.title: Sleepy Boats on the Canal
books.first_page: The sun is going down behind the hills, and the boats on the canal are getting sleepy. The green boat with the striped awning yawns and bumps gently against the wall. The little red rowing boat tucks her oars in close. The long flat barge that carries apples to the market sighs a long, slow sigh. The water goes from blue to silver to deep, deep purple. A heron stands on one leg and closes one eye, then the other. Ropes creak. Lamps flicker on in the windows above. Hush now, boats. Hush now, water. The whole canal is ready for bed.

books.title: Moss the Market Mouse
books.first_page: Moss lived inside a cheese stall in the middle of the market, which sounds like the best home a mouse could ever have. It was not. Every morning the stall keeper, a tall woman with flour on her sleeves, swept out every crumb before Moss could reach it. Every afternoon the cat from the fish stall came to sit beside the cheeses and stare. 'There must be a better stall,' said Moss. So he packed a raisin, a thimble and a piece of string, and he set off down the long row of awnings to visit every stall in the market, one by one.

books.title: The Kite That Wanted to Stay
books.first_page: On the windiest day of spring, a yellow kite with a long ribbon tail flew higher than all the other kites on the hill. It could see the pond and the library roof and the boats in the harbour, small as seeds. When the girl holding its string began to wind it in, the kite pulled back. 'Not yet,' it thought. 'I like it up here.' The girl pulled. The kite tugged. The wind laughed and blew harder. And then, with a small snap, the string came loose, and the yellow kite went sailing away over the rooftops, all on its own.

books.title: Otter Tilly Learns to Float
books.first_page: All the otters in Willow Lake could float on their backs. Tilly's big brother could float and crack a mussel on his tummy at the same time. Tilly's grandmother could float and fall fast asleep. But whenever Tilly lay back in the water, her nose went under and her tail went up and she came up spluttering. 'You are trying too hard,' said Grandmother. 'How can I try less?' asked Tilly. Grandmother smiled. 'Tomorrow,' she said, 'I will show you. But first you must find me the flattest, smoothest stone on the whole shore.'

books.title: A Bed for Bramble Bear
books.first_page: Bramble Bear was very tired, and winter was coming, and he did not have a bed. He tried the hollow log by the stream, but it was full of beetles having a party. He tried the soft moss under the pine tree, but it dripped on his nose all night. He tried a pile of leaves in the park, but children kept jumping into it, shrieking with joy. 'Oh dear,' said Bramble Bear, and he yawned the biggest yawn of the year. Then a small voice said, 'Excuse me. I know a place.' It was a robin, sitting on the gate.

books.title: The Snail's Long Afternoon
books.first_page: Shelly the snail had a plan. She would cross the garden path, from the lettuce bed to the strawberry bed, before the sun went down. It was not far for a person. A person could do it in two steps. But for Shelly it was a great journey. She passed a pebble as big as a hill. She passed an ant carrying a crumb as big as a house. She stopped to rest beneath a dandelion, and a bumblebee landed beside her. 'Where are you going in such a hurry?' asked the bee. Shelly was so surprised that she pulled her horns right in.

books.title: Ferry Cat of Saltwick Harbour
books.first_page: Every ferry in Saltwick Harbour has a captain, a bell and a cat. The cat on the blue ferry is called Pickle. Pickle has crossed the bay eleven thousand times, and she has never once been seasick. She knows which passengers have sardine sandwiches. She knows which coil of rope is warmest in the sun. She knows when a storm is coming, because her whiskers tingle. And this morning, as the ferry pulled away from the jetty, Pickle's whiskers were tingling so hard that she leapt onto the captain's hat and would not come down.

books.title: Rain Boots for Grandpa Heron
books.first_page: Grandpa Heron had stood in the cold pond every morning for sixty years, and his feet were tired of it. 'I would like some boots,' he announced one day. The frogs laughed. The ducks laughed. Even the fish, who were not supposed to be listening, made little laughing bubbles. But Grandpa Heron's granddaughter did not laugh. She flew all the way across the commons to the cobbler's shop by the canal, landed on the windowsill and tapped on the glass with her beak. The cobbler looked up from his bench. 'Well,' he said. 'What can I do for you?'

books.title: The Library Owl
books.first_page: High on the top shelf of the library, behind the big atlases, there lives an owl. Her name is Mrs Quill, and her job is to keep the library quiet. When someone drops a book, she ruffles her feathers. When someone giggles, she clicks her beak. When someone sneezes, she says 'Shhh' so softly that it sounds like the pages turning. But one rainy afternoon, a little boy came in who was too sad to make any noise at all. He sat in the corner under the window, and Mrs Quill found that the quiet was not the right kind of quiet anymore.

books.title: Little Fox and the Lost Star
books.first_page: Little Fox was counting the stars above the hills when she noticed that one was missing. It had been right there yesterday, just to the left of the moon, a tiny bright one that always winked at her. Now there was only a dark gap. 'Mama,' she said, 'a star has fallen out of the sky.' Her mother was already asleep. So Little Fox crept out of the den, past the sleeping rabbits, past the old stone wall, and down the hillside towards the lake, because if a star had fallen, she thought, it would surely have landed somewhere soft.

books.title: Wren Builds a Garden
books.first_page: Wren was six years old and she lived on the top floor of a yellow house with no garden at all. There was only a balcony the size of a doormat, with one cracked pot and nothing in it. On Saturday Wren went to the market with her uncle, and the seed seller gave her a paper twist of seeds for free. 'What will they grow into?' asked Wren. The seed seller winked. 'That,' she said, 'is the best part. You will have to wait and see.' Wren held the packet very carefully all the way home.

books.title: The Night the Pond Sang
books.first_page: It began with one frog. Just one, sitting on a lily pad in the middle of the pond, singing a single deep note. Then a second frog joined in, a little higher. Then the crickets in the long grass started their scratchy tune, and the reeds began to whisper, and the water lapped against the stones in time. The children in the courtyard houses sat up in their beds. They opened their windows. They tiptoed out in their pyjamas and gathered on the bank. Nobody spoke. And the pond sang on, louder and sweeter, all through the warm summer night.

books.title: Clementine's Cafe for Bees
books.first_page: Clementine ran the cafe on the corner, and she made the best honey cake in the whole village. But this summer, something was wrong. Fewer bees came to the flowers in her window boxes. The honey jars at the market were getting smaller and dearer. 'If the bees are hungry,' Clementine said to her cat, 'then they need a cafe too.' The cat did not answer, because cats rarely do. But Clementine had already found a pencil, and on the back of a menu she began to draw a plan: tiny tables, tiny cups, and a great many flowers.

books.title: Bun and Beetle Go Camping
books.first_page: Chapter One. The Tent. Bun was a rabbit and Beetle was a beetle, and they were best friends, which surprised everyone except them. One morning Bun said, 'Let us go camping on the hill.' Beetle said, 'I have never been camping.' 'Neither have I,' said Bun. 'That is why we should go.' So they packed a tent, two blankets, a jar of clover jam and a very small torch for Beetle. The hill was steep. Bun hopped. Beetle climbed. By lunchtime they had reached a flat green spot with a view of the whole lake.

books.title: The Tortoise Who Was Always Late
books.first_page: Mortimer the tortoise was late for breakfast. He was late for lunch. He was late for his own birthday party, which everyone agreed was quite an achievement. 'I am not slow,' Mortimer explained. 'I simply notice things.' And it was true. On the way to anywhere, Mortimer noticed the shape of the clouds, the smell of wet stones, the ladybird sleeping on a leaf. One day the whole village planned a picnic by the lake, and everyone said, 'Mortimer, please, please be on time.' Mortimer nodded seriously. He set off at dawn. And then he noticed something.

books.title: Sock the Sheep Climbs a Hill
books.first_page: Sock was the smallest sheep in the meadow, and her wool was so curly that she looked like a cloud that had fallen down. The other sheep were happy to stay in the meadow and eat grass all day. Sock was not. Every morning she looked up at the tallest hill, the one with a single tree on top, and wondered what she could see from there. 'Sheep do not climb hills,' said the oldest ewe. 'Why not?' asked Sock. The oldest ewe thought for a long time. 'I do not remember,' she admitted. So Sock began to climb.

books.title: Lula and the Lighthouse Crab
books.first_page: At the very end of the harbour wall stood a little white lighthouse, and at the bottom of the little white lighthouse lived a crab named Admiral. Lula met him on the first day of the holidays, when she was poking about in the rock pools with her net. He was sitting on a stone, waving one claw at the sea as if he were directing the waves. 'Hello,' said Lula. 'Good morning,' said the crab. 'You are just in time. The light has gone out, and the boats will be coming home tonight.'

books.title: Ten Frogs Go to Sleep
books.first_page: Ten little frogs on a lily pad, croaking at the moon. One hops off to a mossy stone. Now there are nine. Nine little frogs on a lily pad, splashing in the water. One swims off to a hollow reed. Now there are eight. Eight little frogs on a lily pad, catching sleepy flies. One crawls into a flowerpot by the gate. Now there are seven. Seven little frogs on a lily pad, yawning very wide. One slips under a soft green leaf. Now there are six. Can you count them as they go to bed?

books.title: The Bridge Troll's Birthday
books.first_page: Under the humpbacked bridge where the canal meets the river lived a troll called Gudrun. She was big and lumpy and green, and she had a voice like a rumbling cart, so people were a little afraid of her. They crossed the bridge quickly and did not stop to say hello. Gudrun did not mind most days. But tomorrow was her birthday, her four hundredth, and nobody knew. She sat by the water and made a crown out of reeds and put it on her own head. 'Happy birthday, Gudrun,' she said quietly. Up above, someone stopped walking.

books.title: Hazel Counts the Acorns
books.first_page: Hazel the squirrel was getting ready for winter, and she wanted to be very sure she had enough. So she counted. One acorn under the oak. Two acorns by the bench. Three acorns in the flowerbed outside the campus gate. Four, five, six in a row along the wall, like little brown soldiers. She buried each one in a secret place and drew a map in the dirt with her paw. But when the wind blew in the night, the map blew away. In the morning Hazel stood in the middle of the park and scratched her head.

books.title: The Smallest Gardener
books.first_page: In the big community garden behind the library, everyone had a job. Mr Okafor dug the beds. Auntie Sela watered the beans. The twins pulled weeds and argued about whose pile was bigger. And Rosa, who was only four, was given a tiny trowel and told to 'help'. Rosa did not want to help. Rosa wanted her own job. So while the grown ups were busy, she walked to the far corner where nobody went, behind the compost heap, and found a square of earth exactly the right size for a very small gardener. She knelt down. She began.

books.title: Mo the Mole Sees the Sky
books.first_page: Mo the mole had lived his whole life underground. He knew the taste of every kind of soil. He knew the way roots twisted and where the worms liked to gather. But he had never seen the sky. 'What is it like?' he asked a worm. 'Wet,' said the worm, who had been up once in the rain. 'What is it like?' he asked a beetle. 'Big,' said the beetle, and would say no more. So Mo decided to find out for himself. He dug up, and up, and up, until his nose poked out into the middle of the park.

books.title: The Island in the Teacup
books.first_page: Grandma Ivy's teacup had a picture of an island painted on the bottom, with a palm tree and a tiny hut. Theo had seen it a hundred times. But on Tuesday, when he drank the last of his milky tea and looked down, the palm tree was moving. Its leaves were swaying in a breeze. A gull flew across the painted sky. Theo blinked. He looked closer. And then, very suddenly, he was standing on warm sand, with the sound of waves all around him, and a giant pink rim of china curving up into the clouds.

books.title: Canal Light: Small Poems
books.first_page: Morning on the Water. / The canal wakes slowly, rubbing its eyes of light. / A barge yawns past with apples, a gull trails after. / Somebody upstairs is singing to a kettle. / The bridges hold their breath and then let go. / Lock Keeper. / He knows the water's moods the way you know a friend, / when to let it rise, when to ask it to wait. / His hands are rough as rope and twice as patient. / He has never once been in a hurry, / and every boat that passes thanks him for it.

books.title: Songs for a Rainy Window
books.first_page: First Drop. / One drop lands on the glass and wonders where to go. / It wobbles left, it wobbles right, then joins another. / Together they run down, laughing, to the sill. / Puddle Song. / Jump in me, says the puddle, I am deeper than I look. / I have a whole sky inside me, upside down. / I have a cloud, a chimney, and your face. / Indoors. / The rain taps on the roof like small polite fingers. / We do not answer. We are busy with our soup, / and the cat is busy being warm.

books.title: The Pond Keeps Time
books.first_page: Dawn. / The pond is a mirror nobody has looked in yet. / Mist lifts off it like a sheet off a sleeping bed. / A moorhen writes one line across it and is gone. / Noon. / Now the pond is busy: children with jars, / a dog who thinks the ducks are his idea, / a man on the bench who came to read and only watches. / Dusk. / The water takes the colour of the sky and keeps it / a little longer than the sky does, / the way a friend remembers what you said.

books.title: Pockets Full of Weather
books.first_page: What I Keep. / In my left pocket is a piece of wind. / I caught it on the hill and folded it up small. / When I take it out, my hair goes wild. / In my right pocket is a scrap of sun. / It is warm, and a little sticky, like a sweet. / I save it for grey days at school. / Fog. / The fog came down and ate the harbour, / boats and cranes and all. / It was not hungry for long. / By lunch it had given everything back, / a little damp, but none the worse.

books.title: Harbour Lullabies
books.first_page: Rock-a-Boat. / Rock, little boat, on the water so deep, / the lighthouse is blinking to sing you to sleep. / The nets are all folded, the gulls have flown home, / the moon on the waves is a comb in the foam. / Night Ropes. / The ropes creak softly, tied to the rings, / telling each other old harbour things: / the storm of the spring, the calm of the bay, / the fish that got bigger and swam away. / Hush now, says the tide, as it slides from the shore, / I will bring you the morning and nothing more.

books.title: Little Poems About Bread
books.first_page: The Baker at Four. / While the village sleeps, one window is gold. / Inside, a woman folds the dough the way you fold a letter / to someone you love and have not seen in years. / Crust. / Listen. It crackles when you squeeze it, / like footsteps on frost, like a fire just lit. / The first slice is always the best, / and always argued over. / Crumbs. / The sparrows wait on the cafe railing. / They have read the menu. / They know exactly what they want.

books.title: What the Hills Remember
books.first_page: Old Hill. / The hill was here before the village, / before the canal was dug, before the first roof. / It has watched sheep become wool become jumpers / become the elbows of children sliding down it on trays. / It does not mind. It is patient as a grandmother. / The Path. / A path is only a promise many feet have kept. / Nobody planned it. Somebody walked, / and somebody followed, and the grass agreed. / Now it leads to the top, where the wind is waiting / to tell you everything it knows.

books.title: Lantern Verses
books.first_page: Lighting Up. / At six the lamplighter climbs her ladder, / and one by one the street remembers how to glow. / She whistles the same tune every evening. / Nobody knows its name. Everybody knows it. / Paper Lantern. / I made a lantern out of folded paper, / red as a berry, thin as a leaf. / I put a candle in it and it became a small house / with a heart that flickered. / I carried it to the pond and set it down. / It sailed away, still glowing, / like a thought you cannot quite finish.

books.title: Seeds and Other Promises
books.first_page: Planting. / I put a seed in the dark and said, trust me. / It did not answer. Seeds are like that. / I watered it anyway, and waited, / and on the ninth morning it said yes. / Bean. / The bean is climbing the stick / as if it has somewhere important to be. / Every day it reaches a little higher, / curling its green fingers round and round. / I do not know what it is looking for. / I think it might be the sun. / I think it might be me.

books.title: Poems for the Library Steps
books.first_page: Seven Steps. / There are seven steps up to the library door. / On the first you are still outside, thinking about lunch. / By the fourth you can smell the paper. / By the seventh you are already somewhere else, / a desert, a ship, a castle made of snow. / Borrowed. / This book has been to other houses. / Someone read it on a train. Someone spilled tea on page forty. / Someone folded down a corner and never came back. / I unfold it gently. I will keep their place for them.

books.title: Market Morning Rhymes
books.first_page: Up go the awnings, stripy and bright, / out come the apples, rosy and tight. / Here is the cheese man, here is the jam, / here is the lady who sells honey and ham. / Plums in a basket, pears in a row, / carrots still muddy from where they grow. / The Flower Stall. / Tulips in buckets, yellow and red, / daisies for pinning on somebody's head, / one shy sunflower, taller than me, / bowing politely to all who can see. / Count your coins and fill your sack, / the market will be here when you come back.

books.title: A Year of Small Birds
books.first_page: January: Robin. / The robin wears his red like a scarf he will not take off. / He follows the gardener, one hop behind, / hoping for worms and getting them. / February: Blue Tit. / Upside down on the feeder, she does not mind at all. / The world looks just as good from underneath. / March: Wren. / So small, and such a voice! / As if somebody packed a whole choir / into a thimble and then forgot to close the lid. / April: Swallow. / Back from far away, without a map, without a word, / straight to the same barn beam as last year.

books.title: The Quiet Courtyard
books.first_page: Inside the Gate. / Four walls, painted blue and yellow and rust, / and in the middle a fig tree, and under it a bench. / Here the noise of the village stops at the door / like a dog told to wait. / Washing Line. / Shirts wave from window to window, / a conversation of sleeves. / A sock has fallen into the geranium pot. / Nobody will claim it. Nobody needs to. / Evening. / The fountain says the same word over and over. / It is a good word. / I think it means stay.

books.title: Rhymes for Muddy Boots
books.first_page: Squelch. / Into the field and out of the lane, / I went for a walk in the springtime rain. / My boots went squelch and my boots went squash, / and nobody said I needed a wash. / The Ditch. / There is a ditch at the bottom of the hill, / brown as tea and twice as still. / I jumped it once. I jumped it twice. / The third time was not quite so nice. / Home. / Boots by the door in a muddy heap, / socks on the radiator, me asleep.

books.title: Moon Over the Commons
books.first_page: Rising. / The moon comes up behind the campus clock / and for a minute they are the same size, two round faces / deciding which of them is in charge of the night. / The moon wins. It always does. / On the Pond. / The moon lies down on the water to rest. / A duck swims through it and it breaks into coins, / then gathers itself back together, patient, / the way you put a puzzle back after a sneeze. / Last Window. / One window is still lit on the hill. / The moon looks in, kindly, and does not tell.

books.title: The Case of the Missing Bell
books.first_page: The bell on top of the old schoolhouse had rung every morning at eight for as long as anyone could remember. So when the morning came and there was no ring at all, the whole village noticed. Ada Finch noticed first, because she was standing right beneath it, waiting for the sound so she could start her stopwatch. She looked up. The little tower was empty. The rope was still there, swinging gently, but the bell was gone. Ada put her stopwatch in her pocket and took out her notebook instead. Clue one, she wrote: the rope is still warm.

books.title: The Secret of Lock Seven
books.first_page: There are twelve locks on the long canal between the village and the harbour, and every one of them has a keeper's cottage, except Lock Seven. Lock Seven has a cottage, but nobody lives in it. The windows are shuttered. The garden is wild. And yet, said my cousin Benji, someone has been opening the gates at night. 'How do you know?' I asked him. Benji pointed at the water. It was lower on one side than the other, and on the muddy bank, pressed deep, were footprints too small for a grown up and too large for a child.

books.title: The Riddle of the Reading Room
books.first_page: Somebody was leaving notes in the library books. Marigold found the first one on a Wednesday, tucked inside a book about beetles. It was written in green ink, in tiny careful capitals: THE ANSWER IS WHERE THE WATER NEVER FLOWS. She showed it to the librarian, who frowned and said it was probably a joke. But on Thursday there was another, inside a book about knots. And on Friday a third, inside a cookbook, between the pages on gingerbread. Marigold laid all three notes side by side on the long oak table and began to read them again, slowly.

books.title: The Harbour Map Mystery
books.first_page: It was the bottle that was strange first, before the map inside it, because bottles do not usually wash up inside the harbour wall. Kit and Juniper found it wedged between two mooring posts on the morning of the regatta, while everyone else was looking at the boats. The paper was old and soft. It showed the harbour, the lighthouse, the fish market and the three little islands beyond the breakwater, but there was a fourth island drawn on it too, one that neither of them had ever seen. Beside it, someone had marked a cross and written: low tide only.

books.title: The Vanishing Pies of Market Square
books.first_page: Mrs Pennywhistle made twelve pies every Saturday, and every Saturday she sold twelve pies. Until this Saturday, when she counted them out on the stall at seven and there were only eleven. 'I must have miscounted,' she said. At eight there were ten. At nine there were nine. Nobody had paid for them. Nobody had been seen taking them. Her stall was in the middle of the busiest square in the village, with people on every side. My friend Tobias and I watched the stall from behind the flower buckets all morning. At ten, the eighth pie disappeared.

books.title: The Eden Breakfast Book
books.first_page: Breakfast is the meal of beginnings. It is eaten in pyjamas and in a hurry, on doorsteps and on boats, by people who are not yet properly awake. This book gathers the breakfasts I have loved in this village: the porridge from the courtyard house where I grew up, the warm rolls from the bakery by the canal, the fried eggs my neighbour cooks on a little stove on her balcony. None of them are difficult. Start here. Honey Oat Porridge, for two. Put one cup of oats and two cups of milk in a small pan over a low heat, add a pinch of salt, and stir.

books.title: Soups from the Canal Kitchen
books.first_page: Our kitchen sits right on the water, so close that on windy days the steam from the pot drifts out of the window and over the passing boats. Boatmen wave and call out to ask what is cooking. Usually the answer is soup. Soup is forgiving. It waits for you. It stretches to feed one more guest. It uses the carrot that is going soft and the bread that is going hard. These are the soups we make most. Green Pea and Mint. Melt a knob of butter in a pot, soften one chopped onion slowly, then add four cups of peas.

books.title: Market Basket Suppers
books.first_page: Go to the market without a list. That is my only rule. Walk the rows, look at what is shining, ask the grower what is best today, and fill your basket with whatever makes you hungry. Then come home and open this book. Every supper here is built from what a good market offers in its season, and every one can be on the table in under an hour. You will need a sharp knife, a heavy pan and a little patience. Spring Supper: New Potatoes with Herbs and Butter. Scrub a basket of small new potatoes and boil them in salted water until tender.

books.title: Baking with Small Hands
books.first_page: Hello, young baker. This book is for you, and for the grown up who will help with the oven. Before you start, wash your hands, tie back your hair and put on an apron, even a pretend one made from a tea towel. Read the whole recipe first, all the way to the end. Then gather everything you need on the table, so you are not running about with sticky fingers. Mistakes are allowed. Flour on the floor is allowed. First Recipe: Jam Thumbprint Biscuits. You will need one cup of flour, half a cup of soft butter, a spoon of sugar and some jam.

books.title: Picnics for the Hills
books.first_page: A picnic on the hill is worth the climb, but only if everything survives the journey. Soft sandwiches get squashed. Cream melts. Lettuce wilts in the sun. Over many summers of carrying baskets up the long path past the sheep, I have learned which foods travel well and which are best left at home. The recipes in this book are sturdy, cheerful and good to eat with your fingers on a blanket in the wind. Pack a cloth, a knife and a bottle of water. Hill Pasties. Rub butter into two cups of flour until it looks like sand, then add cold water, a spoon at a time.

books.title: Soup for Rainy Thursdays
books.first_page: Every village has a day of the week when the rain seems to settle in on purpose, and in ours it is Thursday. This book began as a list pinned inside my pantry door, a reminder of what to cook when the canals turn grey and the cafe windows fog over. Soup asks very little of the cook. A pot, a knife, a few vegetables past their best, and time. In the pages that follow you will find thirty soups, from a plain leek and potato to a red lentil broth bright with cumin. Each one serves four, or two people twice. Always let a hot pot cool a little before you blend it, and keep small hands well away from the stove.

books.title: The Canal-Side Bakery Book
books.first_page: Our ovens are lit at four in the morning, when the only other people awake are the ducks and the man who sweeps the bridge. I have baked beside the canal for twenty-two years, and people still ask me for the secret of the seeded loaf. There is no secret. There is flour, water, salt, yeast, and the habit of paying attention. Dough tells you when it is ready if you press it gently with a floured finger and watch it spring slowly back. This book collects the recipes we bake every week, written so that a home kitchen can manage them. Start with the plain white loaf in chapter one. Bake it four times before you try anything else.

books.title: A Pantry of Small Jars
books.first_page: Open my cupboard and you will find a crowd of small jars, each with a hand-written label: plum jam, pickled shallots, lemon curd, spiced pears. None of them is large, and that is the point. A small jar is eaten before it can be forgotten, and it makes a fine gift for a neighbour. This book teaches the gentle art of preserving in modest amounts. You will learn to sterilise jars by washing them in hot soapy water and warming them in a low oven, to test a jam's set on a cold saucer, and to store everything in a cool, dark place. Label every jar with its name and the date. Your future self will thank you.

books.title: Bread Before Breakfast
books.first_page: Chapter One. The Overnight Sponge. Most of the work in a good morning loaf happens while you are asleep. Before bed, stir a little flour, water and a pinch of yeast together in a bowl, cover it with a clean cloth and leave it on the kitchen counter. By dawn it will be bubbly and smelling faintly of apples. That is your sponge. Add the rest of your flour, some salt and a splash of warm water, knead for ten minutes, and let it rise while you dress and feed the cat. Shape it, let it rise again, and bake it in a hot oven. Breakfast will be a little late, but it will be worth the wait.

books.title: The Market Cook's Calendar
books.first_page: Introduction. I do not plan my meals at home. I plan them at the market, walking slowly between the stalls with an empty basket and an open mind. What is cheap is usually what is in season, and what is in season usually tastes best. This calendar follows the market year month by month, from the first rhubarb of late winter to the last crates of squash before the frosts. For each month you will find what to look for, how to tell if it is fresh, and three simple dishes to make with it. Talk to the growers. They know which apples keep and which beans need eating tonight, and most of them love to be asked.

books.title: Tea, Toast and Conversation
books.first_page: There is a particular quiet that comes over a table when the toast arrives. Talk stops, butter is passed, and then the conversation begins again, a little warmer than before. I have spent many afternoons at the corner table of our village cafe, and these essays are about the small foods that keep friends sitting together a little longer. Toast, of course, cut into soldiers or triangles depending on the company. Scones, split while still warm. A pot of tea strong enough to stand a spoon in, as my aunt used to say, though I have never seen one actually stand. Pour yourself a cup before you read on. I will wait.

books.title: Twelve Pies for the Harvest Fair
books.first_page: Every autumn the long tables come out on the village green, and every autumn somebody's pie wins the blue ribbon. It has never been mine. This book is my record of twelve years of trying, and I am rather proud of it, because the pies that lost were still delicious. Here are apple and blackberry, pumpkin with nutmeg, a cheese and onion pie for the savoury table, and a pear tart that the judges called 'nearly perfect'. The pastry chapter comes first. Keep your butter cold, handle the dough as little as you can, and let it rest in a cool place before rolling. Then you are ready to bake.

books.title: Cooking for a Courtyard Table
books.first_page: In our part of the village the houses are built around shared courtyards, and on summer evenings the tables are carried out and pushed together until they make one long table under the vines. Nobody cooks everything. One household brings bread, another a salad, and someone always brings too many potatoes. This book is for that kind of meal: dishes that travel well across a courtyard, that can be served warm or cool, and that stretch to feed a few unexpected guests. There are notes on how to share the cooking fairly, and a short chapter on keeping food safe on a hot day. Cover dishes, keep cold things cold, and bring everything inside before the wasps arrive.

books.title: The Forgetful Baker
books.first_page: Wren Albery forgot things. She forgot her keys, the names of the new families on Lantern Lane, and once, memorably, the cake she had promised for the library's birthday. What she never forgot was a recipe. Give her a list of ingredients once and she could bake it blindfolded twenty years later. So when the old cookbook from the cafe went missing on the morning of the spring fair, and every cook in the village was in a flap, it was Wren they came knocking for. She opened the door in her dressing gown, flour already on her elbows, and listened to the whole sorry tale. 'Well,' she said at last, 'I suppose I had better put the kettle on.'

books.title: Lemons, Honey and Thyme
books.first_page: Three ingredients sit on my windowsill all year round: a bowl of lemons, a jar of honey from the hives above the park, and a pot of thyme. Between them they can rescue almost any dish. A squeeze of lemon wakes up a tired stew. A spoon of honey softens a sharp dressing. A few thyme leaves turn plain roast vegetables into something to talk about. This little book gathers forty recipes built around those three flavours, from a warm honey and lemon drink for a sore throat to a thyme-roasted chicken for Sunday lunch. Please remember that honey should never be given to babies under one year old. Everyone else may help themselves.

books.title: Twelve Months in the Pond Garden
books.first_page: January. The beds are bare and the pond is skinned with ice, and this is the month I love best for planning. I sit by the window with seed catalogues, a pencil and last year's notebook, and I remember. The beans did well against the south fence. The carrots sulked in the heavy soil by the gate. The sunflowers were taller than the postman. A gardener's year does not begin with digging; it begins with remembering. In the chapters ahead I will walk you through each month in our village garden, from sowing under glass in early spring to wrapping the fig tree against the frosts. Wherever your plot is, I hope you will find something here to try.

books.title: Beans Climb Toward the Light
books.first_page: Of all the vegetables a beginner can grow, the climbing bean is the most forgiving and the most rewarding. Push a seed into warm soil in late spring, give it a cane to climb, and within weeks it will be twisting upwards as if it had somewhere urgent to be. This guide covers runner beans, climbing French beans and a few old varieties saved by gardeners in our village. You will learn how to build a sturdy wigwam from canes and string, when to sow so that late frosts do not catch your seedlings, and why picking often makes the plants produce more. Water them well at the roots in dry weather, and they will feed you all summer.

books.title: Apples Take Their Time
books.first_page: A fruit tree is a promise you make to the future. You plant it as a slim whip no taller than your shoulder, and for two or three years it gives you nothing but leaves. Then one spring it blossoms, and one autumn you pick an apple from a tree you planted with your own hands. This book is for anyone who wants to plant a small orchard, whether that means five trees in a field or a single pear against a sunny wall. We will look at choosing varieties that suit your soil, planting in the dormant months, staking against the wind, and pruning gently in winter. Above all, we will practise patience.

books.title: Four Beds by the Washing Line
books.first_page: You do not need a field to grow your own food. Most of the vegetables in my kitchen come from four raised beds, each the length of a door, tucked between the washing line and the shed. The trick is to keep the soil rich, plant close, and never leave a space empty for long. When the early lettuces are finished, sow beetroot. When the beetroot comes out, plant winter greens. In this book I share the plans for my four beds through a whole year, with simple drawings of what grows where and when. Build your beds no wider than you can reach across comfortably, so that you never need to step on the soil.

books.title: Seeds Saved in Paper Envelopes
books.first_page: In the drawer of my potting bench there is a shoebox full of paper envelopes, each one labelled in a different hand. Marigolds from my grandmother. Tomatoes from the man who used to keep the allotment by the canal. A blue cornflower given to me by a child at the school fair. Saving seed is one of the oldest kindnesses between gardeners. This book explains how to do it well. Choose healthy plants, let the seeds ripen fully on the stem, dry them on a plate somewhere airy, and store them cool and dry in paper rather than plastic. Write the name and year on every envelope, and share what you can.

books.title: The Compost Heap Speaks
books.first_page: Excuse me. I am the compost heap at the bottom of the garden, and I would like a word. You walk past me every day with your buckets of peelings and your armfuls of weeds, and you never ask how I am. I am warm, thank you. I am busy. Inside me, millions of tiny creatures are turning your leftovers into dark, crumbly soil. I like a mixture: green things such as grass clippings and vegetable scraps, and brown things such as dry leaves, straw and torn cardboard. I do not like meat, cooked food or anything from the dog. Turn me now and then, keep me damp but not soggy, and in a year I will repay you handsomely.

books.title: Sweet Peas and Other Fragrances
books.first_page: Some flowers are grown to be looked at. Others are grown to be smelled, and those are the ones this book is about. On a June evening my garden is thick with scent: sweet peas on their netting, honeysuckle over the gate, night-scented stock by the back step, and the old roses that nobody remembers planting. A fragrant garden is a gift to everyone who passes, and the bees agree. In these chapters I describe forty scented plants, when they flower, where they like to grow and how to cut them for the house. Begin with sweet peas. Sow them in deep pots in autumn or early spring, and pick the flowers often to keep them coming.

books.title: Planting Trees for Grandchildren
books.first_page: My grandfather planted the oak at the top of the park when he was a boy. He never sat in its shade; it was not big enough until long after he was gone. But I have, and so have my children, and I hope theirs will too. This short book is about planting trees that will outlast us. It covers the best time to plant, which is in the cool months when the tree is resting, how to dig a wide shallow hole rather than a deep narrow one, and how to water a young tree through its first dry summers. It also asks you to think about the space a tree will need in fifty years. Plant generously, and leave room to grow.

books.title: Kind Words for Weeds
books.first_page: A weed, my old teacher used to say, is only a plant growing where somebody did not want it. Before you pull up every green thing between your paving stones, take a closer look. Some of these so-called weeds feed butterflies and bees. Some hold the soil together on a slope. Some, like daisies and clover, make a lawn far prettier than grass alone. This guide describes the common wild plants of our gardens and verges, with drawings to help you recognise them. It tells you which are worth leaving and which really do need managing. Please do not eat any wild plant unless an experienced grown-up is certain what it is. Many of them look alike.

books.title: Ferns in the Gloomy Corner
books.first_page: All gardens have a gloomy corner. Mine is the strip behind the shed where the wall of the library blocks the afternoon sun, and for years I ignored it. Then I learned that a great many beautiful plants actually prefer the shade. Ferns unfurl there like green question marks. Foxgloves and hellebores glow in the half-light. Hostas spread their broad leaves, provided the snails leave them alone. This handbook will help you turn your own shady corner into the most restful part of the garden. We begin by looking at the different kinds of shade, dry and damp, light and deep, because each one suits different plants. Some shade plants are poisonous, so wear gloves.

books.title: Tomatoes on a Sunny Wall
books.first_page: There is no taste quite like a tomato picked warm from the plant and eaten standing in the garden. For that, you need sun, and the best place I know is a south-facing wall, which soaks up heat all day and gives it back at night. This guide follows a tomato season from start to finish. Sow seeds indoors in early spring, pot the seedlings on as they grow, and plant them out only when the nights are reliably warm. Tie the stems to stout canes, pinch out the side shoots on tall varieties, and water regularly at the base rather than over the leaves. Feed them once a week when the first fruits set.

books.title: Bulbs in Autumn, Colour in Spring
books.first_page: Planting bulbs is an act of faith. In the grey days of autumn you kneel in the damp grass and push dry brown lumps into the ground, and then you forget about them. Months later, when you have almost given up on spring, green tips appear, and then crocuses, daffodils and tulips burst open as if they had been waiting all winter to surprise you. This book explains which bulbs to plant and when, how deep to set them, and how to plant them in natural drifts rather than straight lines. A good rule is to plant a bulb at about two or three times its own height. Some bulbs are poisonous, so wash your hands afterwards.

books.title: The Rooftop Herb Patch
books.first_page: When I moved into the flat above the cafe, I had no garden at all, only a flat roof with a low wall and a wonderful view of the canals. Now it is home to more than twenty herbs, growing in pots, old crates and a bathtub I rescued from a neighbour's yard. Herbs are ideal for small spaces. Most of them like sun, good drainage and not too much fuss. In this book I share what has thrived on my roof and what has not. Before you begin, make sure your roof is safe to stand on and that heavy pots will not overload it. Keep containers well away from the edge, and always water carefully.

books.title: Mrs Pellow's Prize Marrow
books.first_page: Nobody in Pondside Row could remember a summer when Mrs Pellow had not won the prize for the largest marrow.
