She grew them in a secret bed behind her hollyhocks, fed them on a mixture she would not describe, and sang to them in the evenings, though she denied it. This year, however, there was a newcomer. Young Tobin Ashgrove had moved into the yellow house at the end of the row, and on his first morning he had been seen wheeling a barrow of very good manure past her gate. Mrs Pellow put down her watering can. She narrowed her eyes. 'Well,' she said to the marrow, 'it seems we have a contest.'

books.title: Rain Barrels and Thirsty Roots
books.first_page: Rain falls on our roofs for free, runs down the gutters and, all too often, disappears into the drains. Then, in the dry weeks of summer, we stand with the hose wishing we had kept some. This little guide is about saving water and using it wisely in the garden. It shows how to fit a water butt beneath a downpipe, with a secure lid to keep out leaves and to keep children and animals safe. It explains why a deep soak once or twice a week is better than a light sprinkle every evening, and how a mulch of compost or bark helps the soil hold its moisture. Water early in the morning, at the roots, and your plants will drink well.

books.title: Reading the Harbour Tides
books.first_page: Twice a day the sea comes into our harbour and twice a day it goes out again, and anyone who keeps a boat or walks the shore must learn its habits. This book is a beginner's guide to tides. We start with the simple question of why they happen, the pull of the moon and the sun on the oceans, and move on to reading a tide table: high water, low water, and the hours in between. You will learn why the tide runs fastest in the middle of its rise, and why a spring tide has nothing to do with the season of spring. Before you walk out onto the sands, always check the time of the next high water.

books.title: Knots for Small Hands
books.first_page: Hello, young sailor. Every boat in the harbour is held together, tied up and kept safe by knots, and every knot was learned by someone who started exactly where you are now. In this book you will learn ten useful knots, one at a time. There is the reef knot for tying two ends together, the figure of eight that stops a rope slipping through, the clove hitch for a post, and the bowline, which makes a loop that will not slip or tighten. Each knot has drawings to follow, step by step. Practise with a piece of soft rope at the kitchen table. Never tie a rope around yourself or anyone else.

books.title: Lantern at Gull Point
books.first_page: The lamp at Gull Point had been lit every night for ninety years, and for the last six of them it had been Isla Marrow who climbed the hundred and eight steps to light it. She was eleven when her father first let her carry the lamp, and seventeen now, and she knew every creak of the spiral stair. On the evening the fog came in from the north, thick as wool, she was halfway up when she heard it: a ship's bell, far out on the water, ringing slow and lost. Isla took the last steps as fast as she safely could. Somewhere out there, someone needed the light, and they needed it now.

books.title: First Lessons in a Dinghy
books.first_page: Chapter One. Before You Get Wet. Sailing a small boat is one of the great joys of living by the water, but every good sailor begins on dry land. Before your first lesson you will need a buoyancy aid that fits snugly, shoes that grip, and clothes you do not mind soaking. You will also need a teacher, because nobody should sail alone until they have learned to capsize and right a boat in calm, supervised water. In this chapter we name the parts of a dinghy, from the bow at the front to the transom at the back. We learn where the wind is coming from, and why that matters more than anything else.

books.title: The Mackerel Season
books.first_page: When the elder flowers are out along the harbour road, the old fishermen say, the mackerel are in the bay. I cannot promise the two are connected, but every summer of my life the silver shoals have arrived around the same time as the creamy blossom. This book is a memoir of mackerel summers: fishing from the harbour wall with a simple line, going out in my uncle's open boat at dawn, and cooking the catch on the beach the same evening. It is also a gentle guide for anyone who wants to try. Take only what you will eat, handle the fish kindly, and wear a life jacket whenever you are in a boat.

books.title: Nets, Lines and Patience
books.first_page: My grandmother mended fishing nets on the quay for forty years. She sat on an upturned crate with a wooden needle and a ball of twine, and the nets passed through her hands like water. She used to say that fishing was one part skill, one part luck and eight parts patience. This book is a history of the fishing families of our harbour, told through the tools they used and the stories they told. There are chapters on net making, on the long lines baited for cod in winter, and on the small crab pots that every family seemed to own. Most of all it is about patience, which the sea still asks of us all.

books.title: A Boatbuilder's Notebook
books.first_page: These pages come from the notebook I keep on the bench in my shed by the slipway. They are stained with varnish, smudged with pencil and, in one place, marked with a perfect ring where I put down a cup of tea. I build small wooden rowing boats, one or two a year, the old way: planks bent over moulds, fastened with copper nails, the seams made tight by the swelling of the wood. I have tried to set down how it is done, from choosing timber to the first launch. Woodworking tools are sharp and need care. Learn alongside an experienced builder, wear eye protection, and never hurry a cut.

books.title: The Fog Over Brindle Bay
books.first_page: On the morning the fog came, Pip Calloway woke to find the harbour gone. Not gone exactly, for she could hear it, the slap of water on the wall and the creak of ropes, but the world outside her window had turned white and soft and silent, like the inside of a cloud. Her brother Ned was already at the door with his boots on. 'The ferry hasn't come in,' he said. 'Mum says it should have docked an hour ago.' Pip pulled on her jumper. Down on the quay, a little crowd of grown-ups stood staring into nothing, and the harbour master was ringing the old brass fog bell, slow and steady.

books.title: Shells of the Eastern Shore
books.first_page: Walk along the eastern shore at low tide and you will find the sand scattered with treasure. Cockles ribbed like tiny fans. Mussels blue-black and shining. Periwinkles, limpets, the pale spiral of a whelk, and, if you are very lucky, the pink inside of a scallop shell. This field guide will help you name what you find. Each page shows a shell from above and below, with notes on the creature that lived inside it and where it is usually found. Please collect only empty shells, leave living creatures where they are, and put stones back the way you found them. Keep an eye on the incoming tide as you walk.

books.title: Clouds Over the Harbour Wall
books.first_page: Long before there were forecasts, sailors read the sky. They watched the clouds thicken from high wisps to heavy grey, noticed when the wind backed or veered, and felt the change in the air before a squall. Some of their old sayings are nonsense, and some are surprisingly wise. This book sorts one from the other. It explains how clouds form, what a halo around the moon may tell you, and why a falling barometer is worth paying attention to. But let me be clear from the first page. Old signs are a pleasure to learn and a useful extra, not a replacement. Always check the proper forecast before you go out on the water.

books.title: The Harbour Ferry's Long Day
books.first_page: At six o'clock in the morning, when the gulls were still yawning, the little harbour ferry woke up with a cough and a splutter. Her name was Bramble, and she was painted green and yellow, with a red funnel and a brass bell that went ding. 'Good morning, harbour,' said Bramble. 'Good morning, Bramble,' said the harbour, in a sleepy slosh. Bramble had a busy day ahead. She had to carry the baker's bread across to the island, take the school children to their nature walk, and bring home the old fisherman and his dog. And at the very end of the day, there was a special surprise waiting, though Bramble did not know it yet.

books.title: Gulls, Terns and Cormorants
books.first_page: Stand on the harbour wall for five minutes and you will see more birds than you can count. Gulls wheeling and squabbling over the fishing boats. Terns hovering above the water and then dropping like thrown darts. A cormorant on a post with its wings spread out to dry, looking for all the world like a little black umbrella. This guide introduces the seabirds of our coast, how to tell them apart and what each one is doing. It also asks for good manners. Please do not feed the gulls, keep well back from nesting birds in spring, and use a pair of binoculars rather than walking closer for a better look.

books.title: Rowing Home at Dusk
books.first_page: I learned to row in the summer I turned ten, in a heavy old boat called the Dorrie that my father kept tied to a ring in the harbour wall. The oars were taller than I was. For the first week I went mostly in circles, while the fishermen leaned on the rail and offered advice I did not want. Then one evening it clicked: the long pull, the lift, the reach forward again. I rowed us home across the still water as the sun went down behind the hills, my father beside me in his life jacket, and he said nothing at all, which from him was the highest praise. These are the stories of that summer and the many evenings since.

books.title: Mending Sails in Winter
books.first_page: When the boats are hauled out and the harbour is quiet, the sail loft comes alive. This is the season for mending. Every sail that went out in summer comes back with something to tell: a frayed edge, a worn patch where it rubbed against the rigging, a small tear from a sudden gust. In this practical book I show how to inspect a sail on a clean dry floor, how to stitch a simple patch by hand with a palm and needle, and how to store sails so they stay sound until spring. The work is slow and quiet, and good for thinking. Put the kettle on, spread out the canvas, and let us begin.

books.title: Charts of the Quiet Coast
books.first_page: A sea chart is not like a map of the land. It tells you less about what you can see and more about what you cannot: the depth of the water, the rocks hidden beneath it, the channels where a boat may safely pass. This book introduces the charts of our own stretch of coast, from the harbour mouth around the headland to the sheltered cove beyond the point. We will learn the symbols for buoys and beacons, read the soundings, and trace a safe course on paper. Studying charts at the kitchen table is good practice, but real passages should always be planned with an experienced skipper and up-to-date charts.

books.title: Twelve Walks Around Eden Pond
books.first_page: Every walk in this book begins and ends at the same place: the stone bench beside the pond, where the ducks gather and the willows dip their branches into the water. From there, paths lead out in every direction, through the commons, along the canals, up into the hills and down to the harbour. Some of these twelve walks take twenty minutes. One, the Long Loop, takes most of a day. Each has a simple map, a description of what you will see, and a note of places to rest. Wear comfortable shoes, carry water, and tell someone where you are going. Then get up from the bench, and set off.

books.title: The Hill Path Companion
books.first_page: The hills above the village are not high, but they are steep in places, and the view from the top is worth every puffing step. This companion is meant to be carried in a coat pocket. It describes the main paths onto the hills, the landmarks along the way, and the plants and birds you are likely to meet. It also contains a few sensible rules. Check the weather before you climb, because cloud can come down quickly and hide the path. Wear boots with a good grip. Take a warm layer even on a sunny day, and something to eat. Stay on the marked paths, and turn back if you are tired. The hill will still be there tomorrow.

books.title: Lakes You Can Walk Around
books.first_page: There is something deeply satisfying about walking all the way around a lake. You set off with the water on your left, and the far shore looks impossibly distant. An hour or two later you are standing on that far shore looking back at where you started, and then, almost without noticing, you are home again. This book describes eight lakes in the country beyond the hills, each with a path that circles its shore. Some are flat and easy enough for small children; others climb over rocky headlands. Keep dogs on a lead near grazing animals, take your litter home, and never swim in cold lake water alone.

books.title: How to Read a Footpath Map
books.first_page: Chapter One. What the Lines Mean. A map is a picture of the land seen from far above, squeezed down so that it fits in your pocket. Once you can read one, you will rarely be lost for long. In this chapter we start with the simplest things. The thin brown lines that curl across the page are contours; each one joins places of the same height, and where they crowd together the ground is steep. Dashed lines show footpaths. Blue is water, green is woodland, and small black squares are buildings. Lay your map flat, turn it until the paths on the paper line up with the paths in front of you, and look around.

books.title: Boots, Bread and a Flask
books.first_page: I have walked these hills for thirty years, and I have learned that a good day out depends less on the route than on what is in your bag. This book is about the small preparations that make walking a pleasure. How to choose boots that fit, and how to break them in gently before a long walk. What to pack: a waterproof, a warm layer, a map, a little first aid kit, plenty of water and something good to eat. My own favourite is a thick slice of bread, a wedge of cheese, an apple and a flask of hot tea. Sit on a dry rock with a view, unwrap your lunch, and you will understand.

books.title: Walking the Canal Towpaths
books.first_page: The canals were dug long ago to carry goods through the village on slow, flat-bottomed boats pulled by horses. The horses walked alongside on a path beside the water, and that path is still there. Today it belongs to walkers, cyclists, anglers and ducks. This guide follows every towpath in and around Eden, from the busy stretch past the market to the quiet reaches where the canal slips out into the fields. Along the way you will pass locks, bridges, old warehouses and the lock keeper's cottage with its painted door. Towpaths are flat and easy, but the edges can be slippery, so keep small children close to you.

books.title: The Ridge at First Light
books.first_page: I set my alarm for half past four and lay awake for most of the hour before it rang. Outside, the village was dark and still; only the bakery window glowed on the corner of the square. I let myself out quietly, walked through the sleeping streets, past the campus and the dark library, and found the start of the ridge path by the light of a small torch. The air smelled of dew and cut grass. By the time I reached the first stile, the sky behind the hills had turned the colour of a ripe peach. I did not hurry. I wanted to arrive at the top at exactly the right moment.

books.title: Rambles for Rainy Days
books.first_page: Introduction. Most walking guides assume that the sun is shining. This one does not. Rain is a fact of life in our village, and I have come to believe that some walks are actually better in it. The woods smell richer. The waterfalls in the park roar instead of trickling. The harbour turns silver and grey, and you have the paths almost to yourself. In these pages you will find fifteen short rambles chosen for wet weather: sheltered under trees, close to a warm cafe, and never too muddy. Wear a good waterproof and boots, keep away from streams that are running high, and promise yourself a cup of cocoa at the end.

books.title: A Walker's Guide to Stiles and Gates
books.first_page: You can learn a great deal about a landscape from the way people have crossed its walls and hedges. A ladder stile over a high stone wall. A wooden step stile worn smooth by a century of boots. A kissing gate that swings in a small enclosure so that people can pass and sheep cannot. This curious little guide celebrates the stiles and gates of our countryside, with drawings and notes on how each one works. It also explains the walker's oldest rule. Leave every gate as you found it: if it was closed, close it behind you, and if it was open, leave it open, because a farmer may have a reason.

books.title: The Long Way to the Harbour
books.first_page: Grandad Ferris did not believe in shortcuts. 'A shortcut,' he told Mila on the first morning of the summer holidays, 'is a way of missing things.' So when her mother asked them to take a parcel down to the harbour, a walk of fifteen minutes by the straight road, he folded a map, filled a flask and announced that they would go the long way. They went over the hill behind the school, where the larks were singing. They went along the lake shore, where Mila found a feather as blue as the sky. They stopped at the market for plums. And by the time they reached the harbour, the parcel was the least interesting thing they had.

books.title: The Seven Stiles Round
books.first_page: This walk is seven miles long and crosses seven stiles, which is how it got its name, though the fourth stile is really a gate that sticks. Allow a whole morning. Start at the pond's north bench, where the ducks will tell you loudly that you have forgotten bread. Head east along the reed path until the boardwalk ends, then climb the first stile into Hawley's meadow. Keep the hedge on your left. In spring the field is full of cowslips; in autumn, of puddles. Good boots matter more than a good map on this stretch. At the far corner you will see the windmill's sails above the trees, and from there the way is simply uphill.

books.title: Hill Paths Above the Windmill
books.first_page: Introduction. The hills behind the windmill are not high, but they are generous. From the top of Brackle Rise you can see every roof in the village, the long blue line of the canal and, on a clear day, the white masts in the harbour. This little guide describes nine paths, from a twenty minute stroll to a full day's tramp over the three summits. Each route has a sketch map, a note on how steep it gets and the places to rest. Please close gates, keep to the paths when the sheep are lambing and carry water even on cool days. The hills are kind, but they are still hills.

books.title: A Pocket Map of the Lakes
books.first_page: How to read this map. North is at the top, as it should be. Blue is water, green is woodland and the thin dotted lines are footpaths you are welcome to use. The small black squares are huts and boathouses; the circles with a cross are places where the old maps say a chapel stood, though only the stones remain. Each lake is named twice, once with its proper name and once with the name children use, because the children's names are often better. Upper Mere is called the Teacup. Long Water is called the Eel. Contour lines are drawn every ten metres. Where they crowd together, the ground is steep, so slow down and look where you put your feet.

books.title: Towpath Strolls by the Locks
books.first_page: Of all the walks in Eden, the towpath is the flattest and the friendliest. It runs from the harbour basin to the top lock below the hills, a little over four miles, and you can join it at any of the eleven bridges. There is no wrong direction. Walk upstream in the morning and the sun is at your back; walk downstream in the evening and it sets ahead of you, gold on the water. Along the way you will pass narrowboats, herons, the boatyard, the back gardens of the courtyard homes and at least one cat asleep on a roof. Bring a coat. The wind follows the water.

books.title: Evening Rambles for Slow Feet
books.first_page: A note for the reader. This is a book of short walks for people who like to stop. None of them is longer than a mile, all of them have benches, and most of them end near somewhere selling tea. I wrote it after my knees decided they were done with hills, and I discovered that the village is just as lovely at a dawdle. Perhaps lovelier. You notice the moss on the bridge rails, the way the library windows glow at dusk, the swallows over the park. Each ramble is timed for the hour before sunset. Go gently, look up often and do not let anyone hurry you.

books.title: When the Canal Was Dug
books.first_page: Chapter One. The Spade and the Plan. Before there was a canal, there was a marsh, and before anyone dug a single sod, there was an argument. The farmers on the low ground wanted their fields drained. The millers wanted water for their wheels. The fishermen at the harbour wanted a way to bring their catch inland without a cart that lost a wheel every week. It was Agathe Brune, a surveyor with a stubborn chin and a borrowed theodolite, who drew a line that pleased all three. Her plan was pinned to the door of the old meeting barn on a wet spring morning, and the digging began the very next week.

books.title: The Old Market Ledger
books.first_page: For forty-one years the market clerk kept a ledger, and by some small miracle every volume survived. They sit now in the library's back room, bound in brown cloth gone soft at the corners. This book is drawn from their pages. It is not a grand history. It is a history of eggs, of turnips, of a disputed goose and a cheese that was declared too strong to sell. It records the stall rents, the price of wool in a hard winter and the day the clock tower first chimed over the square. Read between the columns of figures and you will find the village, haggling and laughing, just as it does today.

books.title: Sails Over Eden
books.first_page: The windmill on Brackle Rise has been rebuilt three times, and each time the village swore it would be the last. The first mill was a small post mill, wooden from cap to footing, that could be turned by hand to face the wind. It ground barley for bread and burned down in a dry summer when a spark caught the flour dust. The second was taller and made of brick, and it stood for sixty years until a great storm tore away two of its sails. What you see today is the third, built by a whole village of volunteers. This chronicle tells how each one came to be, and who climbed its ladders.

books.title: Harbour Days, Harbour Nights
books.first_page: I was born above a net loft, and the first sound I remember is the harbour bell. My father mended nets and my mother kept the tally of the boats going out and coming in, chalking each name on a slate by the door. If a name stayed on the slate too long after dark, she would put on her coat and walk to the end of the breakwater with a lamp. She never once lost a boat, though there were nights she stood there until morning. These are my memories of the harbour as it was, before the new quay, when every child in the village could tie a bowline.

books.title: How the Library Began
books.first_page: It began with one shelf and a borrowed key. In the year the canal was finished, a schoolteacher named Odile Fenwick noticed that the village owned perhaps two hundred books in total, and that most of them lived in the same three houses. She asked each family to lend one book to a shelf in the meeting barn, to be read by anyone and returned within a fortnight. Forty-three books arrived in the first month, including a cookery book with no cover and a very damp atlas. Within a year there were four shelves, a lending card and a rota of volunteers. Within ten, there was a building.

books.title: A Lamplighter Remembers
books.first_page: Every evening for twenty-two years I walked the same round with a ladder on my shoulder and a long brass pole in my hand. Ninety-six lamps, from the harbour steps to the observatory gate. I knew each one by its quirks. The lamp by the cafe flickered in a north wind. The one on Tanners Bridge always needed a second try. Children followed me on summer nights and counted the lamps aloud, and if they lost count I made them start again. People ask whether I miss it now the lamps light themselves. I miss the quiet, I tell them. And the counting.

books.title: The Courtyard Homes and Their Builders
books.first_page: Introduction. Walk through any arch on Weaver Row and you will find yourself in a courtyard: a square of cobbles, a well or a fountain, a fig tree or a vine, and four households sharing the shade. Nobody planned it this way at first. The earliest houses were built facing the street, each with its back yard walled off from the next. It was the builder Mattias Orley who suggested knocking the walls down and sharing a single garden instead, so that one well could serve many families. His neighbours thought him strange. Within a generation, every new home in Eden was built around a courtyard. This book tells how that happened.

books.title: The Eleven Bridges
books.first_page: There are eleven bridges over the canal, and every one has a story. The Hump is the oldest, built of rough grey stone so steep that carts had to be pushed over it by whoever happened to be passing. Kettle Bridge is named for the tinker who lived beneath it one summer and sold tea to the bargemen. The swing bridge near the boatyard still turns, though it creaks so loudly that the herons leave whenever it moves. In the pages that follow, I have gathered what is known of each bridge: who built it, what it cost, and what the village has called it since.

books.title: The Pond Before the Commons
books.first_page: Long before there were houses, there was the pond. The oldest stories say it was larger then, a shallow lake fringed with willow, and that people came to it in summer to cut reeds for thatch and baskets. Nobody lived beside it all year, because the ground flooded every spring. It was only when the first drainage ditch was cut, generations later, that the land beside the water became dry enough to graze. The villagers agreed that the meadow should belong to no one and to everyone, and so the commons was born. This short history follows the pond and its people through those early centuries.

books.title: Chronicle of the Flood Year
books.first_page: For nineteen days, from the first morning of autumn, the rain did not stop. This is the chronicle of that year, put together from diaries, letters and the memories of those who were children at the time. The canal rose over its banks on the twelfth day. By the fifteenth, boats were rowing down Market Street, and the library had moved its lowest shelves to the upper gallery by a chain of hands. Nobody was lost, which the village still counts as its proudest achievement. When the water finally went down, it left a line of mud on every wall. Some houses still keep it, unpainted, as a reminder.

books.title: The First Cafe on Crooked Lane
books.first_page: My grandmother opened the cafe with one table, two chairs and a stove she bought from a ship's cook. She had no menu. You ate what she had made that morning, and if you did not like it, you were welcome to try the harbour. Fishermen came for the porridge, students came for the warmth and the long hours, and the old men of the village came to argue about the weather. Within a year she needed six tables. Within five, she had knocked through into the bakery next door. This little memoir is her story, as she told it to me over many cups of tea.

books.title: Stargazers on the Hill
books.first_page: Chapter One. A Telescope in a Hen House. The observatory began, as many good things do, in somebody's back garden. Petra Linden was a clockmaker with poor eyesight and an enormous curiosity, and she ground her first telescope mirror by hand over two long winters. Having nowhere else to put it, she set it up in the old hen house at the top of her garden and cut a hatch in the roof. Neighbours came to look at the moon and stayed to look at Saturn. Soon there was a queue on clear nights. When the hen house roof finally fell in, the village decided it was time to build something proper on the hill.

books.title: Founding the Campus
books.first_page: Before it was a school, the campus was nothing of the kind. It began as a set of barns where people gathered on winter evenings to teach one another what they knew. A carpenter taught joinery. A sailor taught knots and navigation. A retired nurse taught how to set a splint and why to wash your hands. Over the years the barns filled up, then overflowed, and the teachers asked the village for a hall. The hall became a quadrangle, the quadrangle gained a library annexe and a laboratory, and somewhere along the way it acquired the motto still carved above its gate: Teach what you know, learn what you don't.

books.title: Gardeners of the Old Commons
books.first_page: Eden has always had more than its share of gardeners. In this book I have tried to gather their stories: the woman who planted the first apple orchard by the park, the boy who saved seeds from every tomato he ever ate, the brothers who quarrelled for thirty years about the correct way to stake beans. Their gardens are mostly gone now, or changed beyond recognition. But their plants are still here. The roses by the library came from one of them. The walnut in the market square came from another. Walk around the village with this book in your pocket and you are walking through their work.

books.title: Letters from the Lock Keeper
books.first_page: Dear Marta, You asked what it is like to keep the top lock, so I shall try to tell you. I rise before dawn, because the first boats come early. I check the gates for leaks and the paddles for stiffness, and I sweep the leaves from the steps so nobody slips. Then I wait. On a busy day I may work the lock forty times, filling and emptying it, raising boats from the low water to the high and lowering them back again. On a quiet day I read, and watch the kingfisher. I think you would like it here. Write soon and tell me about the harbour.

books.title: Dovetails for Patient Hands
books.first_page: Chapter One. Why Dovetails. A dovetail joint is two pieces of wood that hold each other by shape alone. The tails, cut like spread feathers on one board, slide into matching pins on the other, and once they are glued they will not pull apart in the direction of the joint. It is one of the oldest joints there is, and one of the most satisfying to cut. You will need a sharp saw, a sharp chisel, a marking gauge and a great deal of patience. Mark carefully. Cut on the waste side of the line. Clamp your work, keep both hands behind the cutting edge, and never rush. A good joint is slow; a quick one usually needs to be cut again.

books.title: The Knitter's Winter Almanac
books.first_page: November. The nights are drawing in and the wool basket is calling. This is the month to start something warm and simple: a hat in a thick yarn, perhaps, worked in the round on short needles so that you finish before the first frost. If you are new to knitting, begin with a plain stitch and do not worry about evenness. Tension comes with practice, the way handwriting does. Keep a lamp beside your chair, since dark wool is hard to see in the evening. Each month in this almanac has a project, a pattern and a small piece of advice from the knitting circle that meets in the library on Thursdays.

books.title: Clay and the Turning Wheel
books.first_page: Clay is mud with ambitions. Dig it from the right bank, clean out the stones and roots, and you have a material that will take almost any shape you give it, then hold that shape for centuries once it has been fired. This book is for beginners at the wheel. We will start with wedging, which is kneading the clay to push out air bubbles that could crack a pot in the kiln. Then centring, the hardest and most important step, when you press the spinning lump until it runs true beneath your hands. Expect your first dozen pots to collapse. Everyone's do. Keep a bucket of water and a towel within reach, and laugh often.

books.title: Sewing a Book by Hand
books.first_page: Fold a sheet of paper in half and you have a folio. Tuck several folios inside one another and you have a signature. Sew several signatures together along their folds and you have the beginning of a book. That is really all there is to it, and yet there is no end to the ways it can be done. In this first chapter we will make a small notebook with a single signature and a simple pamphlet stitch. You will need paper, a bone folder or the back of a spoon, an awl, a blunt needle and waxed linen thread. Pierce the holes with the awl pointing away from your fingers, and work on a cutting mat.

books.title: Darning, Patching and Other Kindnesses
books.first_page: Holes happen. A hole in a sock is not the end of the sock; it is an invitation. This book is about mending the things we already have: socks and sleeves, elbows and knees, the torn pocket and the lost button. Mending is cheaper than buying new, and kinder to the world, but those are not the best reasons to do it. The best reason is that a mended thing carries a small story. The blue patch on my coat reminds me of the afternoon I fell off the jetty. To begin, find a darning mushroom or a smooth round stone, a blunt needle and some wool in any colour you like.

books.title: Painting the Canal in Watercolour
books.first_page: Watercolour rewards the brave and forgives the patient. You cannot cover a mistake as you can with oils, but you can lift it with a damp brush, or let it dry and paint over it with something darker. The canal is a perfect subject for learning, because water is mostly reflection, and reflection is mostly a softer, darker copy of whatever sits above it. Start with three colours only: a warm yellow, a blue and a red. Mix everything else from those. Wet your paper, lay a pale wash of sky across the top and let it run into the water below. Then sit back and wait. Waiting is half of painting.

books.title: Scales Before Breakfast
books.first_page: Every musician I have ever admired practised scales, and every one of them complained about it. This book is for anyone who plays an instrument, or wants to, and who suspects that practice could be more pleasant than it is. My first rule is short sessions. Fifteen minutes every day will carry you further than two hours on a Sunday. My second rule is to play slowly. If you cannot play a passage slowly and evenly, you cannot really play it fast; you can only hurry through it. My third rule is to stop while you are still enjoying yourself, so that tomorrow you look forward to beginning again.

books.title: Carving Spoons from Green Wood
books.first_page: Green wood is freshly cut wood that still holds its sap, and it is far softer to carve than wood that has dried. A branch of birch, cherry or sycamore, as thick as your wrist and a little longer than your forearm, will make a fine first spoon. Ask before you cut, and only take from a tree that is already being pruned. You will need a small straight knife and a hook knife for the bowl. Before anything else, learn the safe grips described in the next chapter, and always cut away from your body and your other hand. A thumb guard and a cut-resistant glove are worth every coin they cost.

books.title: Weaving on a Frame Loom
books.first_page: Weaving is the art of crossing threads. The threads that run up and down are the warp; you stretch them tight on the loom before you begin. The threads that run side to side are the weft, and you pass them over and under the warp, row after row, until a cloth appears. A simple frame loom can be made from an old picture frame and a row of small nails. In this chapter we will warp one together, and weave a little square that might become a coaster, a patch or a gift. Do not pull the weft too tightly, or your neat square will slowly turn into an hourglass.

books.title: Dyeing Wool with Garden Plants
books.first_page: The yellow of weld, the soft pink of avocado skins, the deep brown of walnut husks: all of these can be coaxed into wool with nothing more than heat, water and time. Plant dyeing is old and gentle work, but it does call for a few sensible habits. Keep a separate pot and spoon for dyeing, and never use them for cooking again. Work in a well aired room or outdoors. Wear gloves, because some dyes stain skin for days. Most importantly, find out what a plant is before you boil it, since a few common garden plants are poisonous. The first recipe in this book uses onion skins, which are safe, free and surprisingly golden.

books.title: Mending Chairs and Stools
books.first_page: Introduction. Somewhere in your house there is a chair that wobbles. Perhaps you have folded a piece of card under one leg, or learned to sit on it carefully, leaning a little to the left. This book will show you how to fix it properly. Most wobbly chairs are suffering from a loose joint, where the glue has dried out and the wood has shrunk. The cure is to take the joint apart, clean off the old glue, and fit it back together with fresh glue and a clamp. It sounds daunting, but it is mostly a matter of patience, a soft mallet and a clear table to work on.

books.title: The Fiddle in the Kitchen
books.first_page: Lesson one: before you play a note, learn to hold the bow. Rest your thumb, bent slightly, against the frog where the hair begins, and let your fingers drape over the stick like a hand resting on a table. Nothing should be tight. A tense hand makes a thin, scratchy sound; a loose hand lets the bow sink into the string and sing. Practise this hold in front of a mirror for a few minutes each day before you even lift the fiddle. It feels silly. Do it anyway. The fiddlers who play at the harbour on summer nights all began exactly here, in somebody's kitchen, with a pencil instead of a bow.

books.title: Baskets from Willow Withies
books.first_page: Willow grows fast and bends without breaking, which makes it the basket maker's best friend. Long, straight shoots called withies are cut in winter when the leaves have fallen, then dried and stored in bundles. Before weaving, soak them in water until they are supple again, roughly a day for every foot of length. In this chapter we will make a small round base, called a slath, by crossing withies and binding them together. It will look nothing like a basket at first. Trust it. Keep a pair of sharp secateurs nearby, cut away from yourself and work outside if you can, because willow is wonderfully messy.

books.title: Sketching People in the Market
books.first_page: Bring a small book and a soft pencil, find a seat near the fruit stalls and look. That is the whole method, really. People in markets move quickly and never pose, so you will learn to draw the gesture first: the curve of a back lifting a crate, the tilt of a head choosing apples. Give yourself thirty seconds for each figure. Do not erase. If a line goes wrong, draw a better one beside it. After a morning you will have pages of half finished people, and some of them will be wonderful. Always ask before you sketch a child, and show anyone your drawing if they are curious.

books.title: Quilts from Leftover Cloth
books.first_page: Scraps are treasure. My grandmother never threw away a piece of fabric. She kept them in a tin, sorted by colour, and every winter she turned them into a quilt. This book is how she taught me to do the same. A quilt has three layers: a pieced top, a soft middle called the batting, and a plain back. The layers are held together by lines of stitching, which is the quilting itself. We will begin with the simplest pattern of all, squares sewn in rows. Press each seam flat with a warm iron as you go, and the squares will line up far better than you expect.

books.title: Why the Stars Seem to Turn
books.first_page: Go outside on a clear night and find a bright star near a rooftop or a tree. Look again an hour later, and it will have moved. All the stars do this, wheeling slowly across the sky from east to west, as though painted on the inside of a great turning bowl. But the stars are not really moving across our sky at all. It is the Earth that turns, spinning once on its axis roughly every twenty-four hours and carrying us with it. In the northern sky there is one star that hardly seems to move, because the Earth's axis points almost straight at it. Sailors once steered by it. You can too.

books.title: What the Clouds Are Saying
books.first_page: Clouds are made of water, but not of rain. Each one is a crowd of tiny droplets or ice crystals, far smaller than a grain of sand, floating on the air. They form when warm, moist air rises and cools, because cool air cannot hold as much water vapour as warm air can. The extra vapour condenses onto specks of dust and salt, and a cloud appears. From the harbour wall you can watch this happen on a summer afternoon, as puffy cumulus clouds build over the hills. Learn their shapes and you can read the coming weather. High, wispy cirrus often means a change is on its way.

books.title: Birds of Pond and Hedge
books.first_page: Sit still by the pond for ten minutes and you will meet more birds than you expect. The first to arrive are usually the ducks, who have learned that people mean bread, although bread is not good for them; a handful of oats or chopped lettuce is kinder. Then, if you are patient, the smaller birds return to the hedges. Listen before you look. Many birds are easier to hear than to see, and each kind has its own song. In this book every bird has a picture, a description of its call and a note on where to find it, from the reed beds to the tops of the willows.

books.title: Life in a Drop of Pond Water
books.first_page: Take a jar to the pond, dip it among the weeds and hold it up to the light. Tiny specks will be swimming in it, jerking and darting. Those are water fleas, and they are only the beginning. Put a single drop under a microscope and a whole world appears: single-celled creatures that glide by waving thousands of tiny hairs, green algae shaped like stars and crescents, and rotifers with spinning crowns that sweep food into their mouths. Many of these living things are made of just one cell, yet they eat, move and multiply. Always wash your hands after handling pond water, and return your jar to the pond when you are done.

books.title: Stones Underfoot
books.first_page: Pick up any pebble from the lake shore and you are holding a story millions of years long. Geologists sort rocks into three great families. Igneous rocks formed from melted rock that cooled, either deep underground or after pouring from a volcano. Sedimentary rocks built up in layers, from sand, mud or shells settling at the bottom of ancient seas and lakes, and were slowly pressed into stone. Metamorphic rocks began as one of the other kinds and were changed by enormous heat and pressure without melting. The grey stone of the Hump bridge is sedimentary; look closely and you may see the faint lines of its layers, or even a tiny fossil shell.

books.title: The Quiet Work of Bees
books.first_page: A honeybee colony is one family of many thousands, living together in a single hive. Nearly all of them are female worker bees. There is one queen, who lays the eggs, and in summer a few hundred males, called drones. A worker's job changes as she grows older. Young bees clean cells and feed the larvae; middle aged bees build comb and guard the entrance; the oldest fly out to gather nectar and pollen. When a forager finds good flowers, she returns and performs a dance on the comb, and its direction and length tell her sisters where to fly. If a bee lands on you, stay calm and still. It will usually fly away.

books.title: Your Beating Heart
books.first_page: Put two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist, just below the thumb, and you will feel it: a small, steady tap. That is your pulse, the wave of pressure sent through your arteries each time your heart squeezes. Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist, and it has been beating since before you were born. It has four chambers. The right side pumps blood to your lungs to collect oxygen; the left side pumps that fresh blood all around your body. At rest, an adult's heart beats roughly sixty to a hundred times a minute. Walk briskly up the hill to the observatory and count again.

books.title: Numbers That Grow Like Flowers
books.first_page: Start with one and one. Add them, and you get two. Add the last two numbers again, one and two, and you get three. Keep going: five, eight, thirteen, twenty-one. This sequence, where each number is the sum of the two before it, turns up in surprising places in the garden. Count the spirals on the face of a sunflower or the scales of a pine cone, going one way and then the other, and you will very often find two neighbouring numbers from the list. Many flowers have three, five or eight petals. Nobody planted these numbers there. They arise from the simple way a plant adds each new seed or leaf as it grows.

books.title: How the Wind Turns the Mill
books.first_page: Why does a windmill turn? Wind is simply air on the move, and moving air carries energy. When it strikes the angled sails of a mill, it pushes them sideways as well as backwards, much as your hand is pushed when you hold it at a slant out of the window of a moving cart. Because the sails are fixed to a central shaft, that sideways push becomes a turning motion. Inside the mill, gears carry the turning down to the millstones, which grind grain into flour. The miller must keep the sails facing into the wind. A mill pointed the wrong way barely moves, which is why the cap of our windmill can rotate.

books.title: A Month of Moons
books.first_page: The Moon makes no light of its own. What we see is sunlight bouncing off its grey, dusty surface. At every moment, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun and half is in darkness, just like the Earth. As the Moon travels around us, taking about twenty-nine and a half days from one new moon to the next, we see different amounts of its sunlit half. When it lies between us and the Sun, the lit side faces away and we see almost nothing: a new moon. When it is on the far side of us from the Sun, we see the whole bright face. Keep a moon diary for a month and watch it change.

books.title: Rain, Rivers and the Sea
books.first_page: Water never really goes away. The sun warms the lakes, the sea and even the puddles on Market Street, and some of that water rises invisibly into the air as vapour. High above, it cools and gathers into clouds. When the droplets in a cloud grow heavy enough, they fall as rain, or as snow in the coldest months. The rain soaks into the hills, trickles into streams and finds its way to the lakes and the canal, and then, at last, out through the harbour into the sea. Then the sun warms it again. Scientists call this endless round the water cycle, and you are part of it every time you drink.

books.title: Seeds and How They Travel
books.first_page: A plant cannot walk, but its children can travel a remarkably long way. Seeds have found dozens of ways to leave home. Dandelion seeds ride the wind on tiny parachutes. Sycamore seeds spin down like little propellers, drifting away from the parent tree as they fall. Burdock burrs hook onto the fur of passing animals, and onto socks. Berries are eaten by birds, and the seeds inside pass through unharmed to land somewhere new. Some pods even burst open with a snap, flinging their seeds across the path. Why go to so much trouble? A seedling that grows far from its parent does not have to compete with it for light and water.

books.title: Light and Rainbows
books.first_page: Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of every colour. You can prove this with a glass of water on a sunny windowsill, or by standing with your back to the sun while someone waters the garden with a fine spray. A rainbow appears whenever sunlight enters raindrops. As the light passes into each drop it bends, and the different colours bend by slightly different amounts, so they spread apart. The light reflects off the back of the drop and bends again on its way out. Red always ends up on the outside of the bow and violet on the inside. Never look directly at the sun while you search for one.

books.title: Tides at the Harbour
books.first_page: Twice a day, the sea creeps up the harbour steps, and twice a day it slips away again. These are the tides, and they are caused mainly by the Moon. The Moon's gravity pulls on the whole Earth, but it pulls a little harder on the side nearest to it and a little less on the far side. The oceans respond by bulging slightly on both sides, and as the Earth turns, each stretch of coast passes through two bulges and two hollows every day. The Sun helps too. When Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the tides run highest and lowest. Fishermen call these spring tides, whatever the season.

books.title: Underground Gardeners
books.first_page: Dig a spadeful of good soil in the vegetable garden and you will almost certainly find an earthworm. It may not look like much, but it is one of the hardest workers in Eden. Earthworms have no eyes, no lungs and no bones. They breathe through their moist skin, which is why they come to the surface after heavy rain. As they tunnel, they swallow soil and fallen leaves, and leave behind crumbly casts rich in nutrients that plants can use. Their burrows let air and water reach the roots. A healthy meadow may hold hundreds of worms beneath every square metre. If you lift one, keep your hands damp and put it back gently.
